A Theory of Saddle Escape in Deep Nonlinear Networks

Divit Rawal Affiliation: Department of Physics Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Affiliation: Berkeley, CA 94720 Email: divit.rawal@berkeley.edu    Michael R. DeWeese Affiliation: Department of Physics Affiliation: Department of Neuroscience Affiliation: Redwood Center Affiliation: University of California, Berkeley Affiliation: Berkeley, CA 94720 Email: deweese@berkeley.edu
Abstract

In deep networks with small initialization, training exhibits long plateaus separated by sharp feature-acquisition transitions. Whereas shallow nonlinear networks and deep linear networks are well studied, extending these analyses to deep nonlinear networks remains challenging. We derive an exact identity for the imbalance of Frobenius norms of layer weight matrices that holds for any smooth activation and any differentiable loss and use this to classify activation functions into four universality classes. On the permutation-symmetric submanifold, the identity combines with an approximate balance law to reduce the full matrix flow to a scalar ODE, giving a critical-depth escape time law τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}) governed by the number rr of layers at the bottleneck scale rather than the total depth LL. We find that this same r−2r-2 exponent is recovered under He-normal initialization with rr bottleneck layers rescaled by ε\varepsilon, where the symmetry manifold is preserved by the flow but not attracting. We find close agreement between our theory and numerical simulations.

1 Introduction

In deep nonlinear networks with all or some layers initialized at small scale, training exhibits saddle-structured dynamics characterized by long plateaus and sharp transitions corresponding to successive feature activation [9, 35]. Recent work has formalized this picture in several ways, including saddle-to-saddle descriptions of training dynamics [1], staircase-style complexity acquisition [2], neural-race reductions for gated networks [34], alternating feature-learning dynamics in two-layer networks [25], and frequency-ordered learning phenomena [31]. These perspectives are largely descriptive or confined to shallow settings, and do not give a sharp dynamical mechanism for the transitions between stages in deep networks with smooth nonlinear activations. General saddle-escape results [23] bound worst-case escape times under generic perturbations but do not use the symmetries that govern stagewise learning in overparameterized deep networks.

Exact theories of learning dynamics fall into three lines of work: the deep-linear line, giving closed-form mode-wise solutions with depth-dependent plateaus [33, 5, 6]; the saddle-to-saddle line, ordering low-rank saddles in deep linear and diagonal-linear networks via balancing and small initialization, with ReLU extensions [21, 30, 24, 10]; and the teacher-student line, reducing high-dimensional dynamics to low-dimensional order parameters under SGD and in mean-field or lazy limits [16, 11, 32, 3, 17, 28, 7, 8, 4, 14]. Much of this work relies on linear or 11-homogeneous structure, shallow architectures, or infinite-width limits.

This work.

We identify a single scalar quantity — the number rr of layers at the small initialization scale, not the total depth LL — that sets the plateau escape time τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}) in deep networks with smooth activations for a single-mode teacher at initialization scale ε\varepsilon. We derive an exact identity for the drift of the layer imbalance, valid for any loss function and activation. A single functional φσ​(z)=z​σ′​(z)−σ⁡(z)\varphi_{\sigma}(z)=z\sigma^{\prime}(z)-\sigma(z) (the pointwise failure of Euler’s identity for σ\sigma) groups activations by the order qq of the first nonlinear term in their Taylor expansion (recovering the linear case of [15, 33]).

Two theoretical arguments predict the same r−2r{-}2 exponent. On the permutation-symmetric submanifold, the identity combines with an approximate balance law to reduce the matrix flow to a one-dimensional integral. Off the manifold at He-normal initialization [18], we work directly with the coordinate-free signal energy γ⁡(W)=𝔼⁡[f​g]\gamma(W)=\mathbb{E}[f\,g]; an AM-GM bound on the layerwise gradient tensors gives the same exponent. The agreement is evidence that rr is a property of the flow, not the reduction.

Contributions.

  • •

    We derive a nonlinear analog of the layer-imbalance conservation law of deep-linear networks, valid for any smooth activation and any differentiable loss, and show that a single functional of the activation classifies deep networks into four dynamical regimes.

  • •

    We reduce gradient flow on the permutation-symmetric submanifold to a one-dimensional integral, and derive a critical-depth escape-time law τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}) set by the number of bottleneck layers rather than the total depth.

  • •

    We lift the r−2r{-}2 exponent off the manifold at He-normal initialization with rr bottleneck layers rescaled by ε\varepsilon via a signal-energy argument on the scalar γ⁡(W)=𝔼⁡[f​g]\gamma(W)=\mathbb{E}[fg], which is independent of any ansatz; this gives the scaling in a regime where the manifold is not attracting.

Setup.

We study LL-layer fully connected feedforward networks f(x)=WLσ(WL−1σ(⋯σ(W1x)))f(x)=W_{L}\sigma(W_{L-1}\sigma(\cdots\sigma(W_{1}x))) with a smooth activation σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, weight matrices Wl∈ℝnl×nl−1W_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{l}\times n_{l-1}} of width n0=dn_{0}=d, n1=⋯=nL−1=Nn_{1}=\cdots=n_{L-1}=N, and scalar output nL=1n_{L}=1. We write zl≐Wl​hl−1z_{l}\doteq W_{l}h_{l-1} for the pre-activations and hl≐σ⁡(zl)h_{l}\doteq\sigma(z_{l}) for the post-activations with h0=xh_{0}=x. Inputs are Gaussian x∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), training is by gradient flow W˙l=−∇Wlℒ\dot{W}_{l}=-\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L} on the population squared loss ℒ⁡(W)=12​𝔼x,y​[(f⁡(x)−y)2]\mathcal{L}(W)=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{x,y}[(f(x)-y)^{2}], and the target is a single-hidden-layer teacher with r∗r^{*} orthonormal modes y=∑k=1r∗βk​σ​(vk⊤​x)y=\sum_{k=1}^{r^{*}}\beta_{k}\sigma(v_{k}^{\top}x), β1>β2>⋯>βr∗>0\beta_{1}>\beta_{2}>\cdots>\beta_{r^{*}}>0, producing the characteristic sequence of r∗r^{*} saddles separating the stagewise modes. Sections 3 and 4 specialize to the single-mode case r∗=1r^{*}=1; the multi-mode teacher returns in Section 5.

2 Imbalance Identity and Activation Classes

Before proceeding to the scalar reduction of the gradient flow ODE, we present an exact identity that holds for the full network, for any smooth activation, and for any differentiable loss. It controls the evolution of the layer imbalance Δl≐‖Wl+1‖F2−‖Wl‖F2\Delta_{l}\doteq\|W_{l+1}\|_{F}^{2}-\|W_{l}\|_{F}^{2} and identifies a functional of the activation that dictates whether layer norms are conserved, drift at cubic order, or drift at quadratic order.

Theorem 1 (Imbalance identity).

Let σ∈C1​(ℝ)\sigma\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}), let ℒ=𝔼(x,y)​[ℓ⁡(f⁡(x,W),y)]\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}[\ell(f(x;W),y)] for any differentiable per-example loss ℓ\ell, and consider the gradient flow W˙l=−∇Wlℒ\dot{W}_{l}=-\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}. Define

φσ​(z)≐z​σ′​(z)−σ⁡(z),\varphi_{\sigma}(z)\doteq z\sigma^{\prime}(z)-\sigma(z), (1)

extended entrywise to vectors. Then for each l∈{1,…,L−1}l\in\{1,\dots,L-1\},

dΔldt=2​𝔼​[⟨Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ,φσ​(zl)⟩],\derivative{\Delta_l}{t}=2\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl\langle W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l})\bigr\rangle\right], (2)

where ∇zl+1ℓ\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell denotes the per-example gradient of ℓ⁡(f⁡(x,W),y)\ell(f(x;W),y) with respect to the pre-activation zl+1​(x,W)z_{l+1}(x;W), and the expectation is over (x,y)(x,y).

A full proof of Theorem 1 is deferred to Section A.1. The identity also lifts to a matrix-valued statement for Wl+1⊤​Wl+1−Wl​Wl⊤W_{l+1}^{\top}W_{l+1}-W_{l}W_{l}^{\top} (Section A.2), recovering the deep linear conservation Wl+1⊤​Wl+1−Wl​Wl⊤=constW_{l+1}^{\top}W_{l+1}-W_{l}W_{l}^{\top}=\mathrm{const} [29, 22, 5] as the special case φσ≡0\varphi_{\sigma}\equiv 0; a Noether-style view of how such symmetry-induced conservation is broken by discretization and weight decay appears in [27, 37].

Using the identity, we may now classify smooth activations σ\sigma by two indices: whether σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, and the order q≥2q\geq 2 of the first nonlinear term in the Taylor expansion σ⁡(z)=a0+α​z+aq​zq+O⁡(zq+1)\sigma(z)=a_{0}+\alpha z+a_{q}z^{q}+O(z^{q+1}) with aq≠0a_{q}\neq 0. The parameter qq controls both the leading drift order (Proposition 2) and the size of the first universality correction (Corollary 7).

Proposition 2 (Classification of smooth activations).

Let σ∈C∞​(ℝ)\sigma\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) with its derivative σ′​(0)≠0\sigma^{\prime}(0)\neq 0, write q∈{2,3,…}∪{∞}q\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\} for the order of the first nonlinear term of σ\sigma at the origin, and assume σ\sigma is odd, satisfies σ⁡(0)≠0\sigma(0)\neq 0, or satisfies σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0 with σ′′​(0)≠0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)\neq 0. Then exactly one of the following holds:

  • (A)

    q=∞q=\infty (linear): φσ≡0\varphi_{\sigma}\equiv 0 and Δl\Delta_{l} is exactly conserved.

  • (Bq)

    σ\sigma is odd and nonlinear, q∈{3,5,7,…}q\in\{3,5,7,\ldots\}: φσ​(z)=(q−1)​aq​zq+O⁡(zq+2)\varphi_{\sigma}(z)=(q-1)a_{q}z^{q}+O(z^{q+2}). The generic subclass is q=3q=3.

  • (C)

    σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, q=2q=2: φσ​(z)=a2​z2+O⁡(z3)\varphi_{\sigma}(z)=a_{2}z^{2}+O(z^{3}).

  • (D)

    σ⁡(0)≠0\sigma(0)\neq 0: φσ​(0)=−σ⁡(0)≠0\varphi_{\sigma}(0)=-\sigma(0)\neq 0 (constant drift, formally q=0q=0).

Representative activations include (A) linear (and a.e. ReLU); (B3) tanh\tanh, erf\mathrm{erf}, sin\sin; (C) GELU, Swish; (D) sigmoid, softplus. We state all downstream results in terms of qq for generality, but most activations of interest are q=3q=3. Proofs follow by Taylor expansion (Section A.5). We note that Theorem 1 couples φσ​(zl)\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l}) to a backprop factor, so global control of φσ\varphi_{\sigma} alone does not bound the drift; in the small-initialization regime this factor stays Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), making qq the main structural prediction.

For the remainder of this work we specialize to Class B activations under a symmetric balanced ansatz where the restriction of eq. 2 to the ansatz manifold is sharper: the drift scales as εL+2\varepsilon^{L+2} in the layer initialization scale ε\varepsilon, higher order than the layer scales themselves.

3 Scalar Reduction on the Symmetric Manifold

Theorem 1 is sharpest when evaluated on a flow-invariant manifold: the same type of reduction performed in deep-linear theory via Wl+1⊤​Wl+1−Wl​Wl⊤≡0W_{l+1}^{\top}W_{l+1}-W_{l}W_{l}^{\top}\equiv 0. Our Class B analog is the following.

Definition 3 (Symmetric balanced ansatz).

There exist scalars X1,…,XL≥0X_{1},\ldots,X_{L}\geq 0 and a unit vector w^∈ℝd\hat{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the input direction, such that every neuron in each layer ll shares the same row of the weight matrix, with scale XlX_{l}:

  • •

    Layer 11: each row of W1W_{1} equals X1​w^∈ℝdX_{1}\hat{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

  • •

    Layers 2≤l≤L−12\leq l\leq L-1: every entry of WlW_{l} equals Xl/NX_{l}/N.

  • •

    Output layer LL: every entry of WLW_{L} equals XL/NX_{L}/\sqrt{N}.

The ansatz is the SNS_{N}-fixed-point manifold of hidden-neuron permutation symmetry [12, 36]: for a single-mode teacher with Gaussian inputs and population squared loss, the data, loss, and teacher are all invariant under permutation of the NN neurons in any hidden layer, so the gradient flow preserves the submanifold on which every neuron in a given layer shares one row. Flow-invariance (Section B.1) and the scalar readout structure it forces make this the nonlinear counterpart of exact balance in deep-linear theory. The normalization absorbs the layer-11 width factor (‖W1‖F2=N​X12\|W_{1}\|_{F}^{2}=NX_{1}^{2}, ‖Wl‖F2=Xl2\|W_{l}\|_{F}^{2}=X_{l}^{2} for l≥2l\geq 2), so the XℓX_{\ell} live on a common Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) scale. On the manifold, the normalized scalar imbalance Δ~ℓ≐‖Wℓ‖F2/cℓ−‖W1‖F2/c1\widetilde{\Delta}_{\ell}\doteq\|W_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}/c_{\ell}-\|W_{1}\|_{F}^{2}/c_{1} with c1=Nc_{1}=N, cℓ=1c_{\ell}=1 (ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2) reduces exactly to Xℓ2−X12X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2}; this is the ansatz analog of the matrix imbalance of eq. 2.

Throughout this section we fix a single-mode teacher y=β1​σ​(v1⊤​x)y=\beta_{1}\sigma(v_{1}^{\top}x) with w^=v1\hat{w}=v_{1} and an activation σ⁡(u)=α​u+aq​uq+O⁡(uq+1)\sigma(u)=\alpha u+a_{q}u^{q}+O(u^{q+1}), with q≥2q\geq 2 the order of the first nonlinear correction (q=3q=3 for Class B, q=2q=2 for Class C). Proofs of SNS_{N}-fixed-point and flow-invariance, and the descent to a scalar flow, are given in Appendix B.

3.1 The Scalar Chain and the Exact Reduced ODE

Under the ansatz, induction on ll shows that the forward pass collapses to a scalar composition (Appendix B):

f(x)=NXLσ(XL−1σ(⋯σ(X1g))),g≐w^⊤x.f(x)=\sqrt{N}X_{L}\sigma\bigl(X_{L-1}\sigma(\cdots\sigma(X_{1}g))\bigr),\qquad g\doteq\hat{w}^{\top}x. (3)

Because the ansatz is flow-invariant (Section B.1), the population gradient flow on WW descends to a flow on the LL scalars (X1,…,XL)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{L}). The reduction below is stated in the scalar-coordinate Euclidean metric on (X1,…,XL)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{L}); equivalently, the matrix flow W˙ℓ=−∇Wℓℒ\dot{W}_{\ell}=-\nabla_{W_{\ell}}\mathcal{L} restricted to the ansatz induces a preconditioned flow in XX whose layer-dependent width factors we absorb into the normalization of Definition 3.

Theorem 4 (Exact ansatz-reduced ODE).

Under Definition 3, Gaussian inputs, aligned single-mode teacher, and population squared loss, the gradient flow on WW reduces exactly to a flow on (X1,…,XL)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{L}) in the scalar-coordinate metric:

dXℓdt=−𝔼g[(f(g)−β1σ(g))∂Xℓf(g)],ℓ=1,…,L,\derivative{X_\ell}{t}=-\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[(f(g)-\beta_{1}\sigma(g))\partial_{X_{\ell}}f(g)\bigr],\qquad\ell=1,\ldots,L, (4)

with ff as in eq. 3 and the expectation over the scalar g∼𝒩⁡(0,1)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Writing c0≐gc_{0}\doteq g, c1≐X1​gc_{1}\doteq X_{1}g, and cℓ≐Xℓ​σ​(cℓ−1)c_{\ell}\doteq X_{\ell}\sigma(c_{\ell-1}) for the scalar pre-activations of the chain, the chain rule along the composition gives the explicit closed form

∂Xℓf=N​(∏m>ℓσ′​(cm−1)​Xm)​σ​(cℓ−1),1≤ℓ≤L,\partial_{X_{\ell}}f=\sqrt{N}\Bigl(\prod_{m>\ell}\sigma^{\prime}(c_{m-1})X_{m}\Bigr)\sigma(c_{\ell-1}),\qquad 1\leq\ell\leq L, (5)

with the empty-product convention ∂XLf=N​σ​(cL−1)\partial_{X_{L}}f=\sqrt{N}\sigma(c_{L-1}), so eq. 4 is fully explicit in the scalar parameters XX alone. The full derivation is given in Appendix B.

3.2 Leading-Order Origin Expansion

The scalar chain eq. 3 is a composition of multiplications by XℓX_{\ell} and activations α​u+O⁡(uq)\alpha u+O(u^{q}). Expanding around the origin, every monomial in f⁡(X,g)f(X,g) arises from choosing, at each of the L−1L-1 nonlinear activations, either the linear branch α​u\alpha u or a nonlinear insertion of order ≥q\geq q. To assist coordinate-wise expansion we shall use later, we record a useful fact: assigning weight 11 to each XℓX_{\ell} and weight 00 to gg, a monomial whose first nonlinear insertion occurs at the jj-th activation carries weighted XX-degree at least L+(q−1)​jL+(q-1)j, minimized at j=1j=1. The cheapest nonlinear configuration is therefore a single insertion at the earliest activation, with all other activations taken linear.

The first nonlinear insertion contributes at XX-degree

f⁡(X,g)=N​αL−1​(∏m=1LXm)​g+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1),f(X,g)=\sqrt{N}\alpha^{L-1}\Bigl(\prod_{m=1}^{L}X_{m}\Bigr)g+O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}), (6)

and ∂Xℓf=N​αL−1​(∏m≠ℓXm)​g+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−2)\partial_{X_{\ell}}f=\sqrt{N}\alpha^{L-1}(\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m})g+O(\|X\|^{L+q-2}). Substituting into X˙ℓ=β1​𝔼​[σ⁡(g)​∂Xℓf]−𝔼⁡[f​∂Xℓf]\dot{X}_{\ell}=\beta_{1}\mathbb{E}[\sigma(g)\partial_{X_{\ell}}f]-\mathbb{E}[f\partial_{X_{\ell}}f], the teacher term contributes at order L−1L-1 via Stein’s identity hσ≐𝔼g​[g​σ​(g)]=𝔼g​[σ′​(g)]h_{\sigma}\doteq\mathbb{E}_{g}[g\sigma(g)]=\mathbb{E}_{g}[\sigma^{\prime}(g)], while the self-interaction is subleading at 2​L−12L-1. The result is the leading-order expansion about the origin

dXℓdt=K(σ)​∏m≠ℓXm+Rℓ​(X),K(σ)≐β1​hσ​αL−1N,\derivative{X_\ell}{t}=K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}+R_{\ell}(X),\qquad K^{(\sigma)}\doteq\frac{\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}\alpha^{L-1}}{\sqrt{N}}, (7)

with |Rℓ​(X)|=O⁡(‖X‖min⁡(L+q−2,2​L−1))|R_{\ell}(X)|=O(\|X\|^{\min(L+q-2,2L-1)}), simplifying to O⁡(‖X‖L+1)O(\|X\|^{L+1}) for Class B activations. The leading drive K(σ)​∏m≠ℓXmK^{(\sigma)}\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m} is identical across layers; the content of the reduction lies in the differences Xℓ2−X12X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2}, where the ∏m≠ℓ\prod_{m\neq\ell} structure survives into the first nonlinear correction and drives a further cancellation.

Approximate imbalance invariant.

The matrix imbalance of eq. 2 restricts to the scalar differences Dℓ≐Xℓ2−X12D_{\ell}\doteq X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2}, which along eq. 4 drift at rate O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1)O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}) — one order higher than the coordinatewise remainder of eq. 7: the degree-(L+q−2)(L{+}q{-}2) piece of RℓR_{\ell} inherits the ∏m≠ℓ\prod_{m\neq\ell} structure of ∂Xℓf\partial_{X_{\ell}}f and the ℓ\ell-independent scalar in front cancels in 2​Xℓ​Rℓ−2​X1​R12X_{\ell}R_{\ell}-2X_{1}R_{1} (for Class B the drift is thus O⁡(‖X‖L+2)O(\|X\|^{L+2})). This near-balance is what reduces the escape analysis to one dimension: the imbalance stays small over the escape window, so Y≐X12Y\doteq X_{1}^{2} together with the fixed gaps DℓD_{\ell} closes a separable scalar ODE. The formal statement with proof and the normal-form extension are deferred to Sections A.3 and C.

4 Escape Laws and the Critical-Depth Exponent

The near-balance above allows us to reduce the escape-time asymptotics of the LL-dimensional reduced flow of eq. 4 to a one-dimensional quadrature. Two distinct facts contribute. First, one-dimensional quadrature is generic: wherever the analytic reduced field is nonvanishing, the flow-box theorem [13] yields coordinates (U,I1,…,IL−1)(U,I_{1},\ldots,I_{L-1}) in which the flow transverses only UU while the IiI_{i} are invariants, so the escape time is a one-dimensional integral. Second, near the small balanced ray the change of variables takes the specific near-identity shape Uℓ=Xℓ+O⁡(sq)U_{\ell}=X_{\ell}+O(s^{q}), giving the balanced-product flow U˙ℓ=Φ⁡(U)​∏m≠ℓUm\dot{U}_{\ell}=\Phi(U)\prod_{m\neq\ell}U_{m} whose invariants preserve the deep-linear balance law at leading order. Along any orbit the squared differences Uℓ2−U12U_{\ell}^{2}-U_{1}^{2} are exactly constant in the normal-form coordinates, so with U≐U1U\doteq U_{1} and gaps Dℓ≐Uℓ​(0)2−U1​(0)2D_{\ell}\doteq U_{\ell}(0)^{2}-U_{1}(0)^{2} the dynamics collapse to

d​Ud​t=Φ⁡(U,D)​∏ℓ≥2(U2+Dℓ),Φ⁡(U,D)=K(σ)​(1+λ​Uq−1+ρ⁡(U,D)),\frac{dU}{dt}=\Phi(U,D)\sqrt{\prod_{\ell\geq 2}(U^{2}+D_{\ell})},\qquad\Phi(U,D)=K^{(\sigma)}\bigl(1+\lambda U^{q-1}+\rho(U,D)\bigr), (8)

where Φ\Phi is the one-dimensional drive, ρ⁡(U,D)=O⁡(Uq)\rho(U,D)=O(U^{q}), and λ\lambda is the analytic obstruction to full 11-homogeneity of the reduced flow; the same coefficient that, against the U−(L−1)U^{-(L-1)} weight in the escape integrand, produces a resonance at L=q+1L=q+1 where the first correction integrates to log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon). The formal normal form, its construction, and the resonance analysis are developed in Appendix C. Every closed form below is an evaluation of eq. 8.

Theorem 5 (Asymptotic escape-time quadrature near the balanced ray).

Fix an initialization with ‖X‖≤ε\|X\|\leq\varepsilon and X10>0X_{1}^{0}>0, and let tesct_{\mathrm{esc}} be the first time X1X_{1} reaches 11. Then

tesc=∫U01d​UΦ⁡(U,D)​∏ℓ≥2(U2+Dℓ),U0≐U1​(0).t_{\mathrm{esc}}=\int_{U_{0}}^{1}\frac{dU}{\Phi(U,D)\sqrt{\prod_{\ell\geq 2}(U^{2}+D_{\ell})}},\qquad U_{0}\doteq U_{1}(0). (9)

Dropping the ρ\rho remainder and setting Φ≡K(σ)\Phi\equiv K^{(\sigma)} (equivalently, Uℓ=XℓU_{\ell}=X_{\ell}) gives the leading-order quadrature

tesclead=∫Y01d​Y2​K(σ)​Y​∏ℓ≥2(Y+Dℓ),Y0≐(X10)2,t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}}=\int_{Y_{0}}^{1}\frac{dY}{2K^{(\sigma)}\sqrt{Y\prod_{\ell\geq 2}(Y+D_{\ell})}},\qquad Y_{0}\doteq(X_{1}^{0})^{2}, (10)

and tesc=tesclead​(1+o⁡(1))t_{\mathrm{esc}}=t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}}(1+o(1)) as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 on the natural time scale εL−2​K(σ)​tesclead=Θ⁡(1)\varepsilon^{L-2}K^{(\sigma)}t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}}=\Theta(1); equivalently tesclead≍ε−(L−2)/K(σ)t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}}\asymp\varepsilon^{-(L-2)}/K^{(\sigma)}, measured in units of 1/K(σ)1/K^{(\sigma)}. The resonance L=q+1L=q+1 produces an additional (λ/K(σ))​log⁡(1/ε)(\lambda/K^{(\sigma)})\log(1/\varepsilon) correction.

Proof sketch.

Separability of eq. 8 gives eq. 9. For the leading-order statement, Φ⁡(U,D)=K(σ)​(1+O⁡(Uq−1))\Phi(U,D)=K^{(\sigma)}(1+O(U^{q-1})), so on U∈[U0,1]U\in[U_{0},1] with U0=O⁡(ε)U_{0}=O(\varepsilon) the multiplicative error Φ/K(σ)−1\Phi/K^{(\sigma)}-1 is pointwise O⁡(Uq−1)O(U^{q-1}). Integrating against the dominant (L−2)(L-2)-form gives a relative correction that is o⁡(1)o(1) except when the Uq−1U^{q-1} factor in Φ\Phi exactly cancels the UL−1U^{L-1} in the denominator, i.e. at L=q+1L=q+1. The normal-form change of variables U=X+O⁡(sq)U=X+O(s^{q}) shifts the upper integration limit by O⁡(1)O(1); since the integrand at U=Θ⁡(1)U=\Theta(1) contributes O⁡(1)O(1) time, this is negligible compared to the ε−(L−2)\varepsilon^{-(L-2)} total. Quantitative bounds and the resonance analysis are in Appendix C. ∎

We refer to tescleadt_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}} as the closed-form or asymptotic escape time. Setting Xℓ0=εX_{\ell}^{0}=\varepsilon for all ℓ\ell gives Dℓ=0D_{\ell}=0 and reduces eq. 8 to Y˙=2​K(σ)​YL/2\dot{Y}=2K^{(\sigma)}Y^{L/2}. Direct integration from Y0=ε2Y_{0}=\varepsilon^{2} to Y=1Y=1 gives

tesclead,bal​(L,ε)={[K(σ)]−1​log⁡(1/ε),L=2,1−εL−2(L−2)​K(σ)​εL−2,L≥3.t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead,bal}}(L,\varepsilon)=\begin{cases}[K^{(\sigma)}]^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon),&L=2,\\[3.0pt] \dfrac{1-\varepsilon^{L-2}}{(L-2)K^{(\sigma)}\varepsilon^{L-2}},&L\geq 3.\end{cases} (11)

The small-ε\varepsilon escape time is therefore logarithmic in two-layer networks and polynomial ε−(L−2)\varepsilon^{-(L-2)} in networks of depth three or more (Appendix C and Figure 2(a)). The jump at L=3L=3 separates the shallow (logarithmic) and deep (polynomial) scaling regimes.

Critical-depth law.

The polynomial exponent L−2L-2 is not a property of the nominal depth but of the critical depth, defined as the number of layers at the bottleneck scale. Sort initial scales 0<s1≤⋯≤sL0<s_{1}\leq\cdots\leq s_{L} and suppose s1=⋯=sr=εs_{1}=\cdots=s_{r}=\varepsilon while sr+1,…,sL=Θ⁡(1)s_{r+1},\ldots,s_{L}=\Theta(1), with a strict hierarchy sj+1/sj→∞s_{j+1}/s_{j}\to\infty as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 across the boundary j=rj=r. A shell-by-shell evaluation of eq. 9 on intervals [sj2,sj+12][s_{j}^{2},s_{j+1}^{2}] where the integrand behaves as if the network had effective depth jj yields the following law.

Theorem 6 (Critical-depth escape law).

Sort initial scales 0<s1≤⋯≤sL0<s_{1}\leq\cdots\leq s_{L} with s1=⋯=sr=εs_{1}=\cdots=s_{r}=\varepsilon, sr+1,…,sL=Θ⁡(1)s_{r+1},\ldots,s_{L}=\Theta(1), and sr+1/ε→∞s_{r+1}/\varepsilon\to\infty as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 (strict hierarchy). Then

tesclead∼{O⁡(1),r=1,log⁡(1/ε)/[K(σ)​∏i>2si],r=2,ε−(r−2)/[(r−2)​K(σ)​∏i>rsi],r≥3.t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}}\sim\begin{cases}O(1),&r=1,\\[2.0pt] \log(1/\varepsilon)/[K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{i>2}s_{i}],&r=2,\\[2.0pt] \varepsilon^{-(r-2)}/[(r-2)K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{i>r}s_{i}],&r\geq 3.\end{cases} (12)

Balanced initialization is the maximal case r=Lr=L, recovering eq. 11. A single isolated bottleneck layer (r=1r=1) removes ε\varepsilon-dependence entirely: the smooth-activation analog of the get-rich-quick phenomenon [26], in which one narrow layer in an otherwise unconstrained network is enough to trigger fast feature learning. Figure 2(b) shows the predicted slopes across r∈{3,…,6}r\in\{3,\ldots,6\} at fixed L=6L=6.

Proof sketch.

Partition [s12,1][s_{1}^{2},1] into shells [sj2,sj+12][s_{j}^{2},s_{j+1}^{2}]. Under the strict-hierarchy assumption the shells with j<rj<r have zero width (all sj=εs_{j}=\varepsilon). On shell rr, the bottleneck-shell asymptotic gives 1/Y​∏ℓ≥2(Y+Dℓ)=(1+o(1))Y−r/2/∏i>rsi1/\sqrt{Y\prod_{\ell\geq 2}(Y+D_{\ell})}=(1+o(1))Y^{-r/2}/\prod_{i>r}s_{i}; antidifferentiation on [ε2,sr+12][\varepsilon^{2},s_{r+1}^{2}] yields the three cases (r=1r=1: Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), r=2r=2: log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon), r≥3r\geq 3: ε−(r−2)/(r−2)\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}/(r-2)). Later shells contribute O⁡(1)O(1) bounded integrals. Full derivation in Appendix C. ∎

Each layer removed from the bottleneck reduces the polynomial exponent by one: the dominant shell shifts from rr to r−1r-1, changing the antiderivative exponent from −(r−2)-(r-2) to −(r−3)-(r-3). In the extreme case r=1r=1, only one layer lies at the bottleneck scale and the escape integral is Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1).

Universality across activations.

Theorem 5 has a single activation-dependent scalar: the prefactor K(σ)=β1​hσ​αL−1/NK^{(\sigma)}=\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}\alpha^{L-1}/\sqrt{N}. The shape of the escape integral eq. 9 is activation-agnostic, and the first correction is controlled by the single parameter qq, the order of the first nonlinear Taylor term of σ\sigma defined in Proposition 2.

Corollary 7 (Universality across Classes A–C).

Let σ1,σ2\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2} be two Class A, B, or C activations with σi′​(0)=αi≠0\sigma_{i}^{\prime}(0)=\alpha_{i}\neq 0, σi​(0)=0\sigma_{i}(0)=0, and first nonlinear orders q1,q2≥2q_{1},q_{2}\geq 2. For any shared initialization, on the natural time scale the leading-order escape times are related by the single scaling

tesc(σ1)tesc(σ2)=hσ2​α2L−1hσ1​α1L−1​(1+o⁡(1)),\frac{t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{(\sigma_{1})}}{t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{(\sigma_{2})}}=\frac{h_{\sigma_{2}}\alpha_{2}^{L-1}}{h_{\sigma_{1}}\alpha_{1}^{L-1}}(1+o(1)),

independently of the orders q1,q2q_{1},q_{2}. Equivalently, the rescaled trajectory t↦X⁡(t/K(σ))t\mapsto X(t/K^{(\sigma)}) is independent of σ\sigma at leading order. The first subleading correction is universal in form: O⁡(εq−1)O(\varepsilon^{q-1}) for all L≠q+1L\neq q+1, and O⁡(εq−1​log⁡(1/ε))O(\varepsilon^{q-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)) at the single resonance L=q+1L=q+1 (L=4L=4 for Class B, L=3L=3 for Class C).

The parameter qq organizes the two nonlinear classes: Class B (q=3q=3: tanh, erf, sin) has the smallest correction O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}) away from the resonance L=4L=4; Class C (q=2q=2: GELU, Swish) has a next-to-leading factor 1+γC​U1+\gamma_{C}\,U with γC≐3​σ′′​(0)2/[2​α​hσ]\gamma_{C}\doteq 3\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)^{2}/[2\alpha h_{\sigma}], producing an O⁡(γC​ε)O(\gamma_{C}\,\varepsilon) deviation from the master curve (Appendix C). In both cases the correction is the λ​Uq−1\lambda U^{q-1} term in the renormalized quadrature of eq. 8. Figure 3 plots K(σ)​tescK^{(\sigma)}t_{\mathrm{esc}} for five activations: after rescaling, Class B curves collapse onto the master curve with residuals consistent with the O⁡(εq−1)O(\varepsilon^{q-1}) correction. We also note that Class D (σ⁡(0)≠0\sigma(0)\neq 0) reduces to the centered case via σ~=σ−σ⁡(0)\tilde{\sigma}=\sigma-\sigma(0) (treated in Section C.4).

5 Multi-Mode Dynamics and Off-Manifold Corrections

The single-mode theory of Section 4 extends to a multi-mode teacher y=∑k=1r∗βk​σ​(vk⊤​x)y=\sum_{k=1}^{r^{*}}\beta_{k}\sigma(v_{k}^{\top}x) with β1>⋯>βr∗>0\beta_{1}>\cdots>\beta_{r^{*}}>0: each mode kk breaks out along a stage-kk saddle after modes 1,…,k−11,\ldots,k-1 have escaped. At generic Gaussian init, off-manifold corrections are not dependent on the on-manifold dynamics, raising two questions: (i) Does the critical-depth law of Theorem 6 depend on the ansatz, or is it intrinsic to the single-mode observable? (ii) Is the block-aligned ansatz itself an attractor, and what captures the escape-time shift when it is not? Below we resolve (i) affirmatively via a teacher-signal scalar that does not depend on any reduction (Theorem 11); answering (ii) is more involved and is the subject of Appendix E.

Fix an aligned single-mode teacher y=β1​σ​(v1⊤​x)y=\beta_{1}\sigma(v_{1}^{\top}x) and set g≐v1⊤​x∼𝒩⁡(0,1)g\doteq v_{1}^{\top}x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), hσ≐𝔼g​[g​σ​(g)]h_{\sigma}\doteq\mathbb{E}_{g}[g\sigma(g)] (the first Hermite coefficient, positive for any Class B/C/D activation with σ′​(0)≠0\sigma^{\prime}(0)\neq 0). With δℓ≐∇zℓf\delta_{\ell}\doteq\nabla_{z_{\ell}}f the layer-ℓ\ell backprop and hℓ−1h_{\ell-1} the forward activation, define the mode-11 signal energy γ\gamma and teacher-signal gradient tensor GℓG_{\ell}:

γ⁡(W)≐𝔼⁡[f⁡(x)​g],Gℓ​(W)≐𝔼⁡[g​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤]∈ℝnℓ×nℓ−1,\gamma(W)\doteq\mathbb{E}[f(x)g],\qquad G_{\ell}(W)\doteq\mathbb{E}\bigl[g\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell-1}}, (13)

together with T⁡(W)≐∑ℓ‖Gℓ‖F2T(W)\doteq\sum_{\ell}\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2} (aggregate layerwise gradient mass) and M≐maxℓ⁡‖Wℓ‖opM\doteq\max_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}} (bottleneck operator scale). Since ∇Wℓγ=Gℓ\nabla_{W_{\ell}}\gamma=G_{\ell} by the chain rule, γ\gamma is an observable whose dynamics do not depend on any reduction.

Proposition 8 (Signal-energy identity).

On gradient flow of the squared loss with Gaussian inputs and an aligned single-mode teacher,

dγdt=β1​hσ​T​(W)​(1+O⁡(M2))−S⁡(W),S⁡(W)≐∑ℓ=1L⟨Gℓ,𝔼⁡[f​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤]⟩F.\derivative{\gamma}{t}=\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}T(W)\bigl(1+O(M^{2})\bigr)-S(W),\qquad S(W)\doteq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigl\langle G_{\ell},\mathbb{E}[f\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}]\bigr\rangle_{F}. (14)
Definition 9 (Small-signal bootstrap interval).

Fix m0>0m_{0}>0 small and define the bottleneck operator scale and its first exit time

M⁡(t)≐max1≤ℓ≤r⁡‖Wℓ​(t)‖op,τm0≐inf{t≥0:M⁡(t)≥m0}.M(t)\doteq\max_{1\leq\ell\leq r}\|W_{\ell}(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}},\qquad\tau_{m_{0}}\doteq\inf\{t\geq 0:M(t)\geq m_{0}\}. (15)

We work on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}], on which

  1. (i)

    the non-bottleneck stack is operator-norm bounded above and below by a constant c∗​(m0,L,σ)c_{\ast}(m_{0},L,\sigma);

  2. (ii)

    the filtered-composition linear-path expansions of Section B.3 hold with constants in (m0,L,σ)(m_{0},L,\sigma),

all independent of ε\varepsilon, rr. Both hold at He-normal init with probability ≥1−e−c1​N\geq 1-e^{-c_{1}N} (Appendix D).

Lemma 10 (Self-interaction bound).

On the small-signal interval [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}], there is a constant C=C⁡(m0,L,σ)C=C(m_{0},L,\sigma), independent of ε\varepsilon, such that |S⁡(W)|≤C​γ​(W)​T​(W)|S(W)|\leq C\gamma(W)T(W).

The proof of Proposition 8 is chain rule plus Stein’s identity applied to the Hermite decomposition σ⁡(g)=hσ​g+σ⟂​(g)\sigma(g)=h_{\sigma}g+\sigma_{\perp}(g); the proof of Lemma 10 is Cauchy–Schwarz on the Frobenius pairing together with the filtered-composition estimates ‖f‖L2≲∏m=1rym≍|γ|\|f\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\prod_{m=1}^{r}y_{m}\asymp|\gamma| (the lower bound |γ|≳∏mym|\gamma|\gtrsim\prod_{m}y_{m} using the initial-nondegeneracy hypothesis of Theorem 11 and its propagation on the bootstrap interval) and ‖δℓ​hℓ−1⊤‖L2≲∏m≠ℓym≍‖Gℓ‖F\|\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m}\asymp\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}, where ymy_{m} is the bottleneck linear-path gain in layer mm. Both are given in Appendix D. Substituting Lemma 10 into eq. 14 and using γ≤m0r≪1\gamma\leq m_{0}^{r}\ll 1 on the bootstrap interval gives the clean differential inequality

γ˙≥c​T​(W),c=12​β1​hσ,\dot{\gamma}\geq cT(W),\qquad c=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}, (16)

valid on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}] for m0m_{0} small enough.

Theorem 11 (Off-manifold critical-depth exponent, bootstrap form).

Fix r≥3r\geq 3, L≥rL\geq r, a Class B activation σ\sigma, and consider gradient flow of the population squared loss from He-normal initialization with the first rr layers rescaled by ε\varepsilon. Assume the initial teacher-signal projection is nondegenerate, |γ⁡(W⁡(0))|≥cnd​εr|\gamma(W(0))|\geq c_{\mathrm{nd}}\varepsilon^{r} for some cnd>0c_{\mathrm{nd}}>0 independent of ε\varepsilon; this holds with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta at He-normal init for any fixed δ>0\delta>0 by Gaussian anti-concentration (Remark Remark). Under the conditions of Definition 9 on the small-signal interval [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}], the loss-threshold escape time τ⋆\tau_{\star} satisfies

τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2)).\tau_{\star}=\Theta\bigl(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}\bigr). (17)

The shallow-bottleneck corners r∈{1,2}r\in\{1,2\} give τ⋆=Θ⁡(1)\tau_{\star}=\Theta(1) and Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)) respectively and are proved by the same argument with a modified antiderivative (Proposition 23).

Proof sketch.

Upper bound via signal energy. The linear-path expansion of Section B.3 gives ‖Gℓ‖F≍∏m≠ℓym\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\asymp\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m} uniformly in (L,r)(L,r) (with Aj=Wj​Aj−1A_{j}=W_{j}A_{j-1}, Bℓ=Wℓ+1⊤​Bℓ+1B_{\ell}=W_{\ell+1}^{\top}B_{\ell+1}, A0=v1A_{0}=v_{1}, BL=1B_{L}=1), so T⁡(W)≍∑ℓ≤r∏m≠ℓym2T(W)\asymp\sum_{\ell\leq r}\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m}^{2} and AM-GM gives T⁡(W)≳γ2−2/rT(W)\gtrsim\gamma^{2-2/r}. Integrating γ˙≥c​γ2−2/r\dot{\gamma}\geq c\gamma^{2-2/r} from γ⁡(0)=Θ⁡(εr)\gamma(0)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{r}) to γ⋆\gamma_{\star} yields τ⋆≤C+​ε−(r−2)\tau_{\star}\leq C_{+}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}.

Lower bound via bottleneck operator growth. The layerwise gradient bound gives ‖W˙ℓ‖F≤‖∇Wℓℒ‖F≲Mr−1+M2​r−1≲Mr−1\|\dot{W}_{\ell}\|_{F}\leq\|\nabla_{W_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}\|_{F}\lesssim M^{r-1}+M^{2r-1}\lesssim M^{r-1} on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}] (using M≤m0M\leq m_{0}), so the upper Dini derivative of the maximum satisfies D+​M​(t)≤C​M​(t)r−1D^{+}M(t)\leq CM(t)^{r-1}. Since M⁡(0)=Θ⁡(ε)M(0)=\Theta(\varepsilon), integrating d​M/Mr−1dM/M^{r-1} gives τm0≥C−​ε−(r−2)\tau_{m_{0}}\geq C_{-}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}. The filtered expansion also gives ‖f‖L2≲Mr≤m0r\|f\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim M^{r}\leq m_{0}^{r}, so for m0m_{0} small enough the loss stays above its escape threshold throughout [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}]; hence τ⋆≥τm0≥C−​ε−(r−2)\tau_{\star}\geq\tau_{m_{0}}\geq C_{-}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}. Combining bounds yields eq. 17. ∎

Theorem 11 makes the single-mode exponent intrinsic to MM and γ\gamma rather than to any ansatz. The product structure ‖Gℓ‖F≍‖Bℓ‖2​‖Aℓ−1‖2\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\asymp\|B_{\ell}\|_{2}\|A_{\ell-1}\|_{2} is the rank-one Frobenius identity applied to the filtered-composition expansion of Section B.3, and the bootstrap interval [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}] is self-certifying since τm0≥C−​ε−(r−2)\tau_{m_{0}}\geq C_{-}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)} covers the escape window (Appendix D). Prefactors depend on off-manifold geometry; Figure 4 confirms the exponent empirically.

Remark (Prefactor agreement on the SNS_{N} manifold).

The AM-GM step T⁡(W)≥c′​γ2−2/rT(W)\geq c^{\prime}\gamma^{2-2/r} saturates when the linear-path gains y1,…,yry_{1},\ldots,y_{r} are equal, the defining equality of the balanced ansatz. Substituting equal ymy_{m} recovers the Theorem 6 prefactor [(r−2)​K(σ)​∏i>rsi]−1[(r-2)K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{i>r}s_{i}]^{-1} exactly: ansatz and signal-energy bound agree in both exponent and constant when restricted to the manifold. At He-normal init the ymy_{m} are i.i.d. up to an O⁡(1)O(1) factor, so AM-GM is loose by a mode-dependent constant — the source of the unresolved off-manifold prefactor.

Multi-mode geometry.

With r∗r^{*} teacher modes, the natural extension of Definition 3 partitions hidden neurons into r∗r^{*} blocks with the single-mode ansatz imposed inside each. This block-aligned ansatz is preserved by the flow but not attracting at generic Gaussian init: linearizing around the stage-11 saddle gives a positive off-block eigenvalue whenever a mixed on-block/off-block loop gain exceeds 11. This is treated in more detail in Appendix E.

6 Discussion

We have shown that the homogeneity deficit φσ​(z)=z​σ′​(z)−σ⁡(z)\varphi_{\sigma}(z)=z\sigma^{\prime}(z)-\sigma(z) classifies activations into four regimes and controls escape from the zero saddle. On the symmetric submanifold the matrix flow reduces to a one-dimensional integral; off the manifold at He-normal init, a signal-energy argument on γ⁡(W)=𝔼⁡[f​g]\gamma(W)=\mathbb{E}[fg] yields the same exponent τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}), identifying rr as the quantity that sets the plateau. Prior work on deep linear networks exploits the exact conservation law Wℓ+1⊤​Wℓ+1−Wℓ​Wℓ⊤=constW_{\ell+1}^{\top}W_{\ell+1}-W_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{\top}=\mathrm{const}; our identity generalizes it beyond only linear or ReLU activations, setting the escape-time depth-dependence of τ⋆\tau_{\star}.

Our analysis identifies the first mode escape time and provides approximations to successive escape times — an exact theory of modewise escape times in multi-mode teacher-student networks remains open and is an exciting area of future research. We also note that our framework is asymptotic as ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}; understanding training dynamics in arbitrarily large initialization networks is another important avenue for future work. More generally, an ab initio theory of the learning dynamics in deep neural networks remains an important goal for the field.

Appendix A Proof and Extension of Theorem 1

We give the derivation of Theorem 1, state the matrix-valued refinement, and record the almost-everywhere version for ReLU.

A.1 Full Derivation of Theorem 1

Fix a layer index l∈{1,…,L−1}l\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\}. Write ℓ\ell for the per-example loss and ℒ=𝔼⁡[ℓ]\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}[\ell] for the population loss, with expectation taken over the input distribution (and any label noise). The pre- and post-activations are zl=Wl​hl−1z_{l}=W_{l}h_{l-1} and hl=σ⁡(zl)h_{l}=\sigma(z_{l}), with h0=xh_{0}=x the input. We use ⟨A,B⟩F≐tr⁡(A⊤​B)\langle A,B\rangle_{F}\doteq\tr(A^\top B) for the Frobenius inner product and ⊙\odot for the Hadamard (entrywise) product.

Under gradient flow W˙l=−∇Wlℒ\dot{W}_{l}=-\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L},

ddt⁡‖Wl‖F2\displaystyle\derivative{t}\|W_{l}\|_{F}^{2} =ddt⁡tr⁡(Wl⊤​Wl)\displaystyle=\derivative{t}\tr(W_l^\top W_l)
=tr⁡(W˙l⊤​Wl)+tr⁡(Wl⊤​W˙l)\displaystyle=\tr(\dot W_l^\top W_l)+\tr(W_l^\top\dot W_l)
=2​tr⁡(Wl⊤​W˙l)\displaystyle=2\tr(W_l^\top\dot W_l)
=2​⟨Wl,W˙l⟩F\displaystyle=2\langle W_{l},\dot{W}_{l}\rangle_{F}
=−2​⟨Wl,∇Wlℒ⟩F.\displaystyle=-2\langle W_{l},\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}\rangle_{F}.

To prove our claim, all that remains is to express ⟨Wl,∇Wlℒ⟩F\langle W_{l},\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}\rangle_{F} as an expectation in pre-activation space.

The per-example chain rule gives

∇Wlℓ\displaystyle\nabla_{W_{l}}\ell =∇zlℓ⋅hl−1⊤,\displaystyle=\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell\cdot h_{l-1}^{\top},

a rank-one outer product between the upstream gradient ∇zlℓ∈ℝN\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and the downstream activation hl−1∈ℝNh_{l-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Taking the expectation over the data distribution and substituting,

⟨Wl,∇Wlℒ⟩F\displaystyle\langle W_{l},\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}\rangle_{F} =tr⁡(Wl⊤​𝔼​[∇zlℓ⋅hl−1⊤])\displaystyle=\tr\bigl(W_{l}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell\cdot h_{l-1}^{\top}]\bigr)
=𝔼⁡[tr⁡(Wl⊤​∇zlℓ⋅hl−1⊤)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\tr(W_l^\top\nabla_{z_l} \ell\cdot h_{l-1}^\top)\bigr]
=𝔼⁡[tr⁡(hl−1⊤​Wl⊤​∇zlℓ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\tr(h_{l-1}^\top W_l^\top\nabla_{z_l} \ell)\bigr]
=𝔼⁡[tr⁡((Wl​hl−1)⊤​∇zlℓ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\tr((W_l h_{l-1})^\top\nabla_{z_l} \ell)\bigr]
=𝔼⁡[tr⁡(zl⊤​∇zlℓ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\tr(z_l^\top\nabla_{z_l} \ell)\bigr]
=𝔼⁡[⟨∇zlℓ,zl⟩],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell,z_{l}\rangle\bigr],

where between the second and third lines we have used linearity of tr\tr and 𝔼\mathbb{E}, between the third and fourth lines we use cyclicity of the trace, and between the fourth and fifth lines we substitute zl=Wl​hl−1z_{l}=W_{l}h_{l-1}. Combining,

ddt⁡‖Wl‖F2\displaystyle\derivative{t}\|W_{l}\|_{F}^{2} =−2​𝔼​[⟨∇zlℓ,zl⟩].\displaystyle=-2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell,z_{l}\rangle\bigr]. (18)

Backpropagation relates the upstream gradients at adjacent layers. Differentiating hl=σ⁡(zl)h_{l}=\sigma(z_{l}) entrywise and zl+1=Wl+1​hlz_{l+1}=W_{l+1}h_{l},

∇zlℓ\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell =(∂hl∂zl)⊤​∇hlℓ=diag⁡(σ′​(zl))⋅Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ=σ′​(zl)⊙(Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ),\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial h_{l}}{\partial z_{l}}\right)^{\top}\nabla_{h_{l}}\ell=\diag(\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l}))\cdot W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell=\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})\odot\bigl(W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell\bigr),

where the first equality is the Jacobian–vector chain rule, the second uses the Jacobian of σ\sigma applied entrywise (a diagonal matrix with entries σ′​(zl)i\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})_{i}) along with the affine Jacobian of zl+1z_{l+1} in hlh_{l}, and the third rewrites the diagonal multiplication as a Hadamard product.

Take the inner product of the backprop identity with zlz_{l}. Using the Hadamard inner product identity ⟨a⊙b,c⟩=⟨b,a⊙c⟩\langle a\odot b,c\rangle=\langle b,a\odot c\rangle for vectors a,b,c∈ℝNa,b,c\in\mathbb{R}^{N},

⟨∇zlℓ,zl⟩\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell,z_{l}\rangle =⟨σ′​(zl)⊙(Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ),zl⟩\displaystyle=\langle\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})\odot(W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell),z_{l}\rangle
=⟨Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ,σ′​(zl)⊙zl⟩\displaystyle=\langle W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})\odot z_{l}\rangle
=⟨Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ,zl⊙σ′​(zl)⟩.\displaystyle=\langle W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,z_{l}\odot\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})\rangle.

Separately, the forward pass zl+1=Wl+1​σ​(zl)=Wl+1​hlz_{l+1}=W_{l+1}\sigma(z_{l})=W_{l+1}h_{l} gives

⟨∇zl+1ℓ,zl+1⟩\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,z_{l+1}\rangle =⟨∇zl+1ℓ,Wl+1​σ​(zl)⟩=⟨Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ,σ⁡(zl)⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,W_{l+1}\sigma(z_{l})\rangle=\langle W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,\sigma(z_{l})\rangle.

Subtracting the two lines inside the expectation, the common factor Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓW_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell pairs against zl⊙σ′​(zl)−σ⁡(zl)=φσ​(zl)z_{l}\odot\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})-\sigma(z_{l})=\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l}):

𝔼⁡[⟨∇zlℓ,zl⟩]−𝔼⁡[⟨∇zl+1ℓ,zl+1⟩]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell,z_{l}\rangle\bigr]-\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,z_{l+1}\rangle\bigr] =𝔼⁡[⟨Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ,φσ​(zl)⟩].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l})\rangle\bigr].

Applying (18) at layers ll and l+1l+1 and subtracting,

ddt⁡(‖Wl+1‖F2−‖Wl‖F2)\displaystyle\derivative{t}\bigl(\|W_{l+1}\|_{F}^{2}-\|W_{l}\|_{F}^{2}\bigr) =−2​𝔼​[⟨∇zl+1ℓ,zl+1⟩]+2​𝔼​[⟨∇zlℓ,zl⟩]\displaystyle=-2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,z_{l+1}\rangle\bigr]+2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell,z_{l}\rangle\bigr]
=2​𝔼​[⟨Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ,φσ​(zl)⟩],\displaystyle=2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell,\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l})\rangle\bigr],

which is eq. 2. ∎

A.2 Matrix-Valued Refinement of Theorem 1

The rank-one chain-rule step used above lifts without a trace, giving a matrix-valued analog of Theorem 1 whose scalar trace recovers the identity.

Corollary 12 (Matrix-valued refinement).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, with ∇zl+1ℓ\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell denoting the per-example gradient as in Theorem 1,

ddt⁡(Wl+1⊤​Wl+1−Wl​Wl⊤)\displaystyle\derivative{t}\bigl(W_{l+1}^{\top}W_{l+1}-W_{l}W_{l}^{\top}\bigr) =𝔼⁡[Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ⋅φσ​(zl)⊤+φσ​(zl)⋅(Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ)⊤].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell\cdot\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l})^{\top}+\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l})\cdot(W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell)^{\top}\bigr].

Taking the trace of both sides recovers eq. 2. The deep-linear case σ⁡(z)=z\sigma(z)=z gives φσ≡0\varphi_{\sigma}\equiv 0 and reproduces the well-known conservation Wl+1⊤​Wl+1−Wl​Wl⊤=constW_{l+1}^{\top}W_{l+1}-W_{l}W_{l}^{\top}=\mathrm{const}.

The matrix refinement is strictly stronger than Theorem 1: it records the directional structure of the imbalance drift in the N×NN\times N layer space, whereas the scalar identity retains only its trace. Tracking the full matrix is what allows the off-manifold analysis of Section 5 to decompose the drift into distinct channels (on-block versus off-block) rather than a single number.

A.3 Approximate Imbalance Invariant on the Ansatz

The matrix imbalance of eq. 2 restricts to the symmetric balanced ansatz as the scalar differences Dℓ≐Xℓ2−X12D_{\ell}\doteq X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2}. Along the flow of eq. 4, these differences move slowly.

Remark on why the drift is one order smaller than naive bounds predict for deep-interior pairs. The proof of Proposition 13 turns on which monomial dominates RℓR_{\ell}, not just its size. The degree count of Lemma 15 gives the coordinatewise remainder Rℓ​(X)=O⁡(‖X‖min⁡(L+q−2,2​L−1))R_{\ell}(X)=O(\|X\|^{\min(L+q-2,2L-1)}) in eq. 7 (simplifying to O⁡(‖X‖L+1)O(\|X\|^{L+1}) for Class B at L≥2L\geq 2), so termwise multiplication yields the naive bound dd​t​Dℓ=2​Xℓ​Rℓ−2​X1​R1=O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1)\tfrac{d}{dt}D_{\ell}=2X_{\ell}R_{\ell}-2X_{1}R_{1}=O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}). The per-insertion analysis of Section B.3 (eqs. 25 and 26) sharpens the pair-drift story by identifying inside the degree-(L+q−2)(L+q-2) piece of RℓR_{\ell} a single dominant monomial: the one in which the very first activation fires the nonlinear slice ρ⁡(u)=aq​uq+⋯\rho(u)=a_{q}u^{q}+\cdots while activations 2,…,L2,\ldots,L stay linear. That monomial carries the qq-vs-11 derivative asymmetry between ℓ=1\ell=1 (differentiating inside ρ\rho, factor qq) and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 (differentiating outside ρ\rho, factor 11). For pairs (i,j)(i,j) with i,j≥2i,j\geq 2 the factor is the same on both sides, producing exact cancellation and the improved drift O⁡(‖X‖L+q)O(\|X\|^{L+q}) — one full order below the naive rate — as recorded in eq. 28. For the ℓ↔1\ell\leftrightarrow 1 pair the factor mismatch leaves a surviving leading term (1−q)​c​(X)​∏mXm(1-q)c(X)\prod_{m}X_{m} of order ‖X‖L+q−1\|X\|^{L+q-1}, so the naive rate is attained; the proposition below records this rate with the explicit leading scalar.

Proposition 13 (Approximate imbalance invariant).

On the exact ansatz-reduced ODE eq. 4, the layer differences Dℓ≐Xℓ2−X12D_{\ell}\doteq X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2} drift at rate

ddt⁡(Xℓ2−X12)=2​Xℓ​Rℓ​(X)−2​X1​R1​(X)=O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1),\derivative{t}\bigl(X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2}\bigr)=2X_{\ell}R_{\ell}(X)-2X_{1}R_{1}(X)=O\bigl(\|X\|^{L+q-1}\bigr), (19)

sharply, as captured by the explicit leading scalar derived below. For Class B (q=3q=3), the imbalance drift is thus O⁡(‖X‖L+2)O(\|X\|^{L+2}).

Proof.

From eq. 7, dd​t​Xℓ2=2​K(σ)​∏mXm+2​Xℓ​Rℓ​(X)\tfrac{d}{dt}X_{\ell}^{2}=2K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{m}X_{m}+2X_{\ell}R_{\ell}(X); the first term is ℓ\ell-independent and cancels in the difference. The structural feature that controls what survives is the qq-versus-11 derivative difference of the first nonlinear insertion, developed in full in Section B.3: write the leading degree-(L+q−2)(L+q-2) correction to ∂Xℓf\partial_{X_{\ell}}f as a single-insertion term in which activation 11 fires the nonlinear slice ρ⁡(u)=aq​uq+O⁡(uq+2)\rho(u)=a_{q}u^{q}+O(u^{q+2}) and activations 2,…,L2,\ldots,L stay linear. Differentiating in XℓX_{\ell} then treats ℓ=1\ell=1 and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 asymmetrically: X1X_{1} lies inside the ρ\rho-kernel and carries the derivative factor qq, while each XℓX_{\ell} with ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 multiplies ρ\rho linearly and carries factor 11. After the Hermite contraction of Section B.3, this gives

Rℓ(lead)(X)=c(X)∏m≠ℓXm+O(∥X∥L+q−1),c(X)≐β1αL−2aqhσ(q)X1q−1(ℓ≥2),R_{\ell}^{(\mathrm{lead})}(X)=c(X)\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}+O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}),\qquad c(X)\doteq\beta_{1}\alpha^{L-2}a_{q}h_{\sigma}^{(q)}X_{1}^{q-1}\quad(\ell\geq 2),

with the same scalar c⁡(X)c(X) for every ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, whereas R1(lead)=q​c​(X)​∏m≠1Xm+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1)R_{1}^{(\mathrm{lead})}=q\,c(X)\,\prod_{m\neq 1}X_{m}+O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}). Pairs (i,j)(i,j) with i,j≥2i,j\geq 2 therefore cancel exactly: Xi​Ri−Xj​Rj=c⁡(X)​(Xi​∏m≠iXm−Xj​∏m≠jXm)+O⁡(‖X‖L+q)=O⁡(‖X‖L+q)X_{i}R_{i}-X_{j}R_{j}=c(X)(X_{i}\prod_{m\neq i}X_{m}-X_{j}\prod_{m\neq j}X_{m})+O(\|X\|^{L+q})=O(\|X\|^{L+q}), since both monomials equal ∏mXm\prod_{m}X_{m}. The ℓ↔1\ell\leftrightarrow 1 comparison, however, retains the factor mismatch: Xℓ​Rℓ−X1​R1=(1−q)​c​(X)​∏mXm+O⁡(‖X‖L+q)X_{\ell}R_{\ell}-X_{1}R_{1}=(1-q)c(X)\prod_{m}X_{m}+O(\|X\|^{L+q}), which is O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1)O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}) and nonzero for q≥2q\geq 2. The full per-insertion-order bookkeeping ((26) and (28) of Section B.3) confirms that deeper insertions (k≥2k\geq 2) cannot upgrade this rate, so dd​t​(Xℓ2−X12)=O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1)\tfrac{d}{dt}(X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2})=O(\|X\|^{L+q-1}) sharply; the sharpness argument of (24) (with hσ(q)≠0h_{\sigma}^{(q)}\neq 0 for every Class B activation used in this paper) shows the bound is attained, not merely an upper bound. ∎

Proposition 13 is the nonlinear analog of deep-linear balance: the Class B bound holds to order ‖X‖L+2\|X\|^{L+2}, the Class C bound to ‖X‖L+1\|X\|^{L+1}. The Class B exponent is sharper than pointwise control of eq. 2 predicts: on the manifold, Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℒW_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\mathcal{L} aligns with φσ​(zl)\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l}) to produce an extra cancellation, giving O⁡(εL+2)O(\varepsilon^{L+2}) in place of the naive |φσ​(zl)|⋅|Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℒ|=O⁡(ε3)⋅O⁡(εL−3)=O⁡(εL)|\varphi_{\sigma}(z_{l})|\cdot|W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\mathcal{L}|=O(\varepsilon^{3})\cdot O(\varepsilon^{L-3})=O(\varepsilon^{L}). The drift can moreover be removed to all orders by a near-identity change of coordinates into a balanced product normal form U˙ℓ=Ψ⁡(U)​∏m≠ℓUm\dot{U}_{\ell}=\Psi(U)\prod_{m\neq\ell}U_{m}; the formal normal form, the renormalized escape law, and the L=q+1L=q{+}1 resonance are developed in Appendix C. For the escape analysis, the leading-order form of Proposition 13 suffices.

A.4 Almost-Everywhere Extension and ReLU

The entire derivation above uses only almost-everywhere differentiability of σ\sigma: every appearance of σ′\sigma^{\prime} occurs inside a Lebesgue integral (through the data expectation), and the chain rule lifts to the distributional sense. Concretely, if σ\sigma is Lipschitz and piecewise C1C^{1}, Rademacher’s theorem provides an a.e.-defined derivative σ′\sigma^{\prime}, the rank-one chain rule ∇Wlℓ=∇zlℓ⋅hl−1⊤\nabla_{W_{l}}\ell=\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell\cdot h_{l-1}^{\top} holds for almost every input xx, and the Hadamard step ∇zlℓ=σ′​(zl)⊙(Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℓ)\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell=\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})\odot(W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\ell) is then an a.e. equality. Since the measure of pre-activations landing on the null set where σ′\sigma^{\prime} is undefined is zero under any absolutely continuous input distribution (Gaussian in particular), the expectation is unchanged by the choice of representative.

A.5 Proof of the Activation Classification

We prove Proposition 2. Write the Taylor expansion σ⁡(z)=∑k≥0ak​zk\sigma(z)=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}z^{k} with a1=σ′​(0)≠0a_{1}=\sigma^{\prime}(0)\neq 0. A direct computation from φσ​(z)=z​σ′​(z)−σ⁡(z)\varphi_{\sigma}(z)=z\sigma^{\prime}(z)-\sigma(z) gives

φσ​(z)=∑k≥0(k−1)​ak​zk=−a0+∑k≥2(k−1)​ak​zk,\varphi_{\sigma}(z)=\sum_{k\geq 0}(k-1)a_{k}z^{k}=-a_{0}+\sum_{k\geq 2}(k-1)a_{k}z^{k}, (20)

so the linear term (k=1k=1) drops out and φσ\varphi_{\sigma} is determined by the constant term and the post-linear Taylor coefficients.

Mutual exclusivity. Classes (A), (Bq), (C), (D) are pairwise disjoint:

  • •

    (A) requires σ\sigma linear, so ak=0a_{k}=0 for all k≥2k\geq 2; in particular σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, σ′′​(0)=0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)=0, and σ\sigma has no nonlinear term, disjoint from any (Bq), (C), (D).

  • •

    (Bq) requires σ\sigma odd and nonlinear, so a0=0a_{0}=0 and all even a2​k=0a_{2k}=0: disjoint from (C) and (D). Different q∈{3,5,7,…}q\in\{3,5,7,\ldots\} are disjoint by definition (each qq is the smallest odd index with aq≠0a_{q}\neq 0).

  • •

    (C) has σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, disjoint from (D); and σ′′​(0)≠0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)\neq 0 rules out every (Bq) (which forces σ′′​(0)=0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)=0).

Exhaustiveness. Let σ\sigma satisfy the hypothesis. If σ⁡(0)≠0\sigma(0)\neq 0, we are in (D). If σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0 and σ′′​(0)≠0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)\neq 0, we are in (C). The remaining case is that σ\sigma is odd. If σ\sigma is odd and linear, we are in (A). If σ\sigma is odd and nonlinear, all even a2​ka_{2k} vanish and there exists a smallest odd q≥3q\geq 3 with aq≠0a_{q}\neq 0; this qq places σ\sigma in exactly one (Bq).

Taylor forms. Substituting into (20): (A) every aka_{k} for k≠1k\neq 1 vanishes, so φσ≡0\varphi_{\sigma}\equiv 0. (D) k=0k=0 gives φσ​(0)=−a0=−σ⁡(0)≠0\varphi_{\sigma}(0)=-a_{0}=-\sigma(0)\neq 0. (C) a0=0a_{0}=0 and the k=2k=2 term contributes a2​z2=σ′′​(0)2​z2a_{2}z^{2}=\tfrac{\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2}z^{2}. (Bq) a0=a2=⋯=aq−1=0a_{0}=a_{2}=\cdots=a_{q-1}=0 by oddness and minimality of qq, so the k=qk=q term contributes (q−1)​aq​zq(q-1)a_{q}z^{q} with aq=σ(q)​(0)/q!≠0a_{q}=\sigma^{(q)}(0)/q!\neq 0. Oddness of σ\sigma implies φσ\varphi_{\sigma} is odd, so only odd-power corrections appear, giving the O⁡(zq+2)O(z^{q+2}) remainder. ∎

Remark.

The hypothesis excludes a thin family (e.g. σ⁡(z)=z+z4\sigma(z)=z+z^{4}) where σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, σ′′​(0)=0\sigma^{\prime\prime}(0)=0, and σ\sigma is not odd. Such σ\sigma still have φσ\varphi_{\sigma} computable term by term from (20), but the leading order is ≥4\geq 4 and the activation does not match any standard architecture; we therefore restrict to the hypothesis of Proposition 2 throughout, which covers every activation in the paper’s tables.

Appendix B Ansatz Invariance and Scalar Reduction

This appendix collects the proofs underlying Section 3: we verify that the symmetric balanced ansatz of Definition 3 is the SNS_{N}-fixed-point manifold of hidden-neuron permutation symmetry, prove it is flow-invariant under population gradient flow, descend the matrix flow to a scalar flow with unit conversion factors, record the explicit closed form of ∂Xℓf\partial_{X_{\ell}}f that enters eq. 4, and derive the filtered-composition remainder bounds that drive eq. 6, eq. 7, and Proposition 13.

B.1 The Ansatz as SNS_{N}-Fixed-Point Manifold

Fix a hidden layer index l∈{1,…,L−1}l\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\} and let π∈SN\pi\in S_{N} act on WW by simultaneous permutation of the NN hidden neurons in layer ll: the rows of WlW_{l} are permuted by π\pi, and the columns of Wl+1W_{l+1} are permuted by π\pi (with the convention that at l=L−1l=L-1, the scalar readout WL∈ℝ1×NW_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times N} has its NN entries permuted). Under a single-mode teacher y=β1​σ​(v1⊤​x)y=\beta_{1}\sigma(v_{1}^{\top}x) with Gaussian inputs and population squared loss, the data law, the loss, and the teacher are each invariant under this action, so the population loss ℒ\mathcal{L} and its gradient satisfy ℒ⁡(π⋅W)=ℒ⁡(W)\mathcal{L}(\pi\cdot W)=\mathcal{L}(W) and ∇Wℒ​(π⋅W)=π⋅∇Wℒ​(W)\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}(\pi\cdot W)=\pi\cdot\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}(W). The fixed-point set {W:π⋅W=W​ for all ​π∈SN​ acting on any hidden layer}\{W:\pi\cdot W=W\text{ for all }\pi\in S_{N}\text{ acting on any hidden layer}\} is precisely the submanifold on which every neuron in each hidden layer shares the same incoming row and the same outgoing column. Aligning the shared input direction of layer 11 with w^∈ℝd\hat{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (a free unit vector that is flow-invariant for a single-mode teacher with w^=v1\hat{w}=v_{1}), we recover Definition 3. Since the gradient is equivariant under the group action, it is tangent to the fixed-point set, and the flow preserves the manifold. The next lemma records this explicitly by showing that each ∇Wlℒ\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L} inherits the entry-pattern of WlW_{l} itself.

Lemma 14 (Ansatz invariance).

Suppose W⁡(t0)W(t_{0}) satisfies Definition 3 with w^=v1\hat{w}=v_{1} and scalars (X1​(t0),…,XL​(t0))(X_{1}(t_{0}),\ldots,X_{L}(t_{0})). Then the population gradient ∇Wlℒ\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L} shares the ansatz structure: ∇W1ℒ\nabla_{W_{1}}\mathcal{L} has NN identical rows each proportional to v1⊤v_{1}^{\top}; ∇Wlℒ\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L} for 2≤l≤L−12\leq l\leq L-1 has all entries equal; ∇WLℒ\nabla_{W_{L}}\mathcal{L} has all entries equal. Consequently, the gradient flow preserves the ansatz for all t≥t0t\geq t_{0}.

Proof.

By eq. 3, f⁡(x)f(x) depends on xx only through g≐v1⊤​xg\doteq v_{1}^{\top}x, as does the single-mode teacher; hence the residual is a scalar function r⁡(x)=f⁡(x)−β1​σ​(v1⊤​x)=ρ⁡(g)r(x)=f(x)-\beta_{1}\sigma(v_{1}^{\top}x)=\rho(g), and the per-example loss ℓ=12​r​(x)2\ell=\tfrac{1}{2}r(x)^{2} is a function of gg alone. The population gradient is ∇zlℒ=𝔼x​[∇zlℓ]\nabla_{z_{l}}\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[\nabla_{z_{l}}\ell]. We shall proceed by cases, with induction on the internal layers.

Layer 1.

Under the ansatz W1=X1​𝟏N​w^⊤W_{1}=X_{1}\mathbf{1}_{N}\hat{w}^{\top} with w^=v1\hat{w}=v_{1}, so z1=W1​x=X1​(v1⊤​x)​𝟏N=X1​g​𝟏Nz_{1}=W_{1}x=X_{1}(v_{1}^{\top}x)\mathbf{1}_{N}=X_{1}g\mathbf{1}_{N}. Every coordinate of z1z_{1} is identical, so ℓ\ell depends on z1z_{1} only through the scalar X1​gX_{1}g, and ∇z1ℓ=q1​(x)​𝟏N\nabla_{z_{1}}\ell=q_{1}(x)\mathbf{1}_{N} for some scalar q1q_{1} depending on xx only through gg. Then

∇W1ℒ\displaystyle\nabla_{W_{1}}\mathcal{L} =𝔼x​[∇z1ℓ⋅x⊤]=𝟏N​𝔼x​[q1​(g)​x⊤].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}\bigl[\nabla_{z_{1}}\ell\cdot x^{\top}\bigr]=\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbb{E}_{x}\bigl[q_{1}(g)x^{\top}\bigr].

Decompose x=g​v1+x⟂x=gv_{1}+x_{\perp} with x⟂⟂v1x_{\perp}\perp v_{1} and x⟂x_{\perp} Gaussian independent of gg under the isotropic input distribution. Then

𝔼x​[q1​(g)​x⊤]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}\bigl[q_{1}(g)x^{\top}\bigr] =𝔼g​[q1​(g)​g]​v1⊤+𝔼⁡[q1​(g)​x⟂⊤]=𝔼g​[q1​(g)​g]​v1⊤,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[q_{1}(g)g\bigr]v_{1}^{\top}+\mathbb{E}\bigl[q_{1}(g)x_{\perp}^{\top}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[q_{1}(g)g\bigr]v_{1}^{\top},

using independence and 𝔼⁡[x⟂]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{\perp}]=0. Every row of ∇W1ℒ\nabla_{W_{1}}\mathcal{L} is therefore the same scalar multiple of v1⊤v_{1}^{\top}, matching the layer-11 ansatz.

Internal layers 2≤l≤L−12\leq l\leq L-1.

We show by descending induction from layer L−1L-1 that ∇zlℒ=ql​(g)​𝟏N\nabla_{z_{l}}\mathcal{L}=q_{l}(g)\mathbf{1}_{N} for some scalar qlq_{l}. Under the ansatz, every internal WlW_{l} has all entries equal to Xl/NX_{l}/N, so for any vector u∈ℝNu\in\mathbb{R}^{N},

Wl+1⊤​u=Xl+1N​𝟏N​𝟏N⊤​u=Xl+1N​(𝟏N⊤​u)​𝟏N,W_{l+1}^{\top}u=\frac{X_{l+1}}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}u=\frac{X_{l+1}}{N}(\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}u)\mathbf{1}_{N},

a scalar multiple of 𝟏N\mathbf{1}_{N}. The forward pass gives hl−1=cl−1​(g)​𝟏Nh_{l-1}=c_{l-1}(g)\mathbf{1}_{N} for some scalar cl−1c_{l-1} (eq. 3), hence zl=Wl​hl−1=Xl​cl−1​(g)​𝟏Nz_{l}=W_{l}h_{l-1}=X_{l}c_{l-1}(g)\mathbf{1}_{N}. Backprop gives

∇zlℒ\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{l}}\mathcal{L} =σ′​(zl)⊙(Wl+1⊤​∇zl+1ℒ)\displaystyle=\sigma^{\prime}(z_{l})\odot\bigl(W_{l+1}^{\top}\nabla_{z_{l+1}}\mathcal{L}\bigr)
=σ′​(Xl​cl−1​(g))​𝟏N⊙(Xl+1N​𝟏N⊤​(ql+1​(g)​𝟏N))​𝟏N=ql​(g)​𝟏N,\displaystyle=\sigma^{\prime}\bigl(X_{l}c_{l-1}(g)\bigr)\mathbf{1}_{N}\odot\Bigl(\tfrac{X_{l+1}}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}\bigl(q_{l+1}(g)\mathbf{1}_{N}\bigr)\Bigr)\mathbf{1}_{N}=q_{l}(g)\mathbf{1}_{N},

closing the induction (the base case at layer LL is handled below). The gradient in weight space is then

∇Wlℒ=𝔼⁡[∇zlℒ⋅hl−1⊤]=𝔼⁡[ql​(g)​cl−1​(g)]​𝟏N​𝟏N⊤,\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\nabla_{z_{l}}\mathcal{L}\cdot h_{l-1}^{\top}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[q_{l}(g)c_{l-1}(g)\bigr]\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top},

so every entry is the same scalar. This matches the internal-layer ansatz.

Layer LL.

Since f⁡(x)=XL​𝟏N⊤​hL−1/Nf(x)=X_{L}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}h_{L-1}/\sqrt{N} is affine in hL−1h_{L-1}, the one-dimensional output gradient reduces to a scalar and

∇WLℒ=𝔼⁡[r⁡(x)⋅hL−1⊤]/N=𝔼⁡[ρ⁡(g)​cL−1​(g)]​𝟏N⊤/N,\nabla_{W_{L}}\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[r(x)\cdot h_{L-1}^{\top}\bigr]/\sqrt{N}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\rho(g)c_{L-1}(g)\bigr]\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}/\sqrt{N},

again equal across entries. This matches the layer-LL ansatz, gives the induction base case qL=ρ/Nq_{L}=\rho/\sqrt{N}, and closes the backwards induction.

Each ∇Wlℒ\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L} therefore inherits the entry-pattern of WlW_{l} itself, so W˙l=−∇Wlℒ\dot{W}_{l}=-\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L} stays inside the ansatz manifold for all t≥t0t\geq t_{0} as claimed. ∎

B.2 Descent to the Scalar Flow

Because each entry of WlW_{l} is a linear function of the scalar XℓX_{\ell} under the ansatz, the full gradient flow on WW descends cleanly to a gradient flow on (X1,…,XL)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{L}). The scalar flow follows simply by matching the entrywise weight updates to X˙ℓ​∂Wl/∂Xℓ\dot{X}_{\ell}\partial W_{l}/\partial X_{\ell}.

Layer 11.

W1=X1​𝟏N​w^⊤W_{1}=X_{1}\mathbf{1}_{N}\hat{w}^{\top} has ∂W1/∂X1=𝟏N​w^⊤\partial W_{1}/\partial X_{1}=\mathbf{1}_{N}\hat{w}^{\top}, and the entrywise gradient flow W˙1=−∇W1ℒ\dot{W}_{1}=-\nabla_{W_{1}}\mathcal{L} gives

X˙1​𝟏N​w^⊤=−∇W1ℒ=−𝔼g​[q1​(g)​g]​𝟏N​v1⊤.\dot{X}_{1}\mathbf{1}_{N}\hat{w}^{\top}=-\nabla_{W_{1}}\mathcal{L}=-\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[q_{1}(g)g\bigr]\mathbf{1}_{N}v_{1}^{\top}.

Matching on both sides with w^=v1\hat{w}=v_{1} yields

X˙1=−𝔼g[q1(g)g]=−∂X1ℒ=−𝔼g[(f−β1σ(g))∂X1f].\dot{X}_{1}=-\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[q_{1}(g)g\bigr]=-\partial_{X_{1}}\mathcal{L}=-\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[(f-\beta_{1}\sigma(g))\partial_{X_{1}}f\bigr].

Internal layers 2≤l≤L−12\leq l\leq L-1.

WlW_{l} has N2N^{2} entries each equal to Xl/NX_{l}/N, so ∂Wl/∂Xl=𝟏N​𝟏N⊤/N\partial W_{l}/\partial X_{l}=\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}/N. Entrywise, W˙l[i,j]=−∂ℒ/∂Wl[i,j]\dot{W}_{l}[i,j]=-\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_{l}[i,j] gives X˙l/N=−∂ℒ/∂Wl[i,j]\dot{X}_{l}/N=-\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_{l}[i,j] for every (i,j)(i,j). Summing over the N2N^{2} entries,

∑i,jW˙l[i,j]=NX˙l=−∑i,j∂ℒ/∂Wl[i,j]=−N∂Xlℒ,\sum_{i,j}\dot{W}_{l}[i,j]=N\dot{X}_{l}=-\sum_{i,j}\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_{l}[i,j]=-N\partial_{X_{l}}\mathcal{L},

where the last equality uses ∂Xlℒ=∑i,j(1/N)​∂ℒ/∂Wl​[i,j]\partial_{X_{l}}\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i,j}(1/N)\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_{l}[i,j]. Canceling NN gives X˙l=−∂Xlℒ\dot{X}_{l}=-\partial_{X_{l}}\mathcal{L}.

Layer LL.

WLW_{L} has NN entries each equal to XL/NX_{L}/\sqrt{N}, so ∂WL/∂XL=𝟏N⊤/N\partial W_{L}/\partial X_{L}=\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\top}/\sqrt{N}. The analogous entrywise-to-scalar matching gives

∑iW˙L[i]=NX˙L=−∑i∂ℒ/∂WL[i]=−N∂XLℒ,\sum_{i}\dot{W}_{L}[i]=\sqrt{N}\dot{X}_{L}=-\sum_{i}\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_{L}[i]=-\sqrt{N}\partial_{X_{L}}\mathcal{L},

so X˙L=−∂XLℒ\dot{X}_{L}=-\partial_{X_{L}}\mathcal{L} and κL=1\kappa_{L}=1. Combining the three cases,

X˙ℓ=−∂Xℓℒ=−𝔼g[(f−β1σ(g))∂Xℓf],ℓ=1,…,L,\dot{X}_{\ell}=-\partial_{X_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}=-\mathbb{E}_{g}\bigl[(f-\beta_{1}\sigma(g))\partial_{X_{\ell}}f\bigr],\qquad\ell=1,\ldots,L, (21)

which is the exact reduced flow of eq. 4.

Explicit closed form of ∂Xℓf\partial_{X_{\ell}}f.

With the scalar pre-activations c0≐gc_{0}\doteq g, c1≐X1​gc_{1}\doteq X_{1}g, and cℓ≐Xℓ​σ​(cℓ−1)c_{\ell}\doteq X_{\ell}\sigma(c_{\ell-1}) for 2≤ℓ≤L−12\leq\ell\leq L-1 so that f⁡(x)=N​XL​σ​(cL−1)f(x)=\sqrt{N}X_{L}\sigma(c_{L-1}), the chain rule along the composition g↦c1↦⋯↦cL−1↦fg\mapsto c_{1}\mapsto\cdots\mapsto c_{L-1}\mapsto f, together with ∂Xℓcℓ=σ⁡(cℓ−1)\partial_{X_{\ell}}c_{\ell}=\sigma(c_{\ell-1}) from the recursion, yields

∂Xℓf=N​(∏m>ℓσ′​(cm−1)​Xm)​σ​(cℓ−1),1≤ℓ≤L,\partial_{X_{\ell}}f=\sqrt{N}\Bigl(\prod_{m>\ell}\sigma^{\prime}(c_{m-1})X_{m}\Bigr)\sigma(c_{\ell-1}),\qquad 1\leq\ell\leq L,

with the empty-product convention ∂XLf=N​σ​(cL−1)\partial_{X_{L}}f=\sqrt{N}\sigma(c_{L-1}). Substituting into eq. 21 makes eq. 4 fully explicit in the scalar parameters XX alone, and we have completed the proof of Theorem 4.

B.3 Filtered Composition and Remainder Bounds

Write

σ⁡(u)=α​u+ρ⁡(u),ρ⁡(u)=O⁡(uq),\sigma(u)=\alpha u+\rho(u),\qquad\rho(u)=O(u^{q}),

with q=3q=3 for Class B and q=2q=2 for Class C. Assign every scalar XℓX_{\ell} weighted degree 11 and gg weighted degree 00. The reduced pre-activation z~L\widetilde{z}_{L} is a composition of multiplications by XℓX_{\ell} and activations: each monomial in its expansion therefore corresponds to a choice, at each of the L−1L-1 internal activations, of either the linear branch α​u\alpha u or one nonlinear insertion ρ\rho.

Lemma 15 (Filtered composition).

Every monomial in the expansion of z~L\widetilde{z}_{L} whose first nonlinear insertion occurs at the jj-th activation (1≤j≤L−11\leq j\leq L-1) has weighted XX-degree at least L+(q−1)​jL+(q-1)j. Consequently,

f⁡(X,g)=N​αL−1​(∏m=1LXm)​g+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1),f(X,g)=\sqrt{N}\alpha^{L-1}\Bigl(\prod_{m=1}^{L}X_{m}\Bigr)g+O\bigl(\|X\|^{L+q-1}\bigr), (22)
∂Xℓf=N​αL−1​(∏m≠ℓXm)​g+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−2).\partial_{X_{\ell}}f=\sqrt{N}\alpha^{L-1}\Bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}\Bigr)g+O\bigl(\|X\|^{L+q-2}\bigr). (23)
Proof.

A monomial whose first nonlinear insertion is at activation jj contributes X1X2⋯Xj+1X_{1}X_{2}\cdots X_{j+1} from the multiplications up to and including the insertion, then factors of weighted degree qq from ρ\rho (the insertion raises the pre-activation’s XX-degree from jj to q​jqj), then further multiplications by XmX_{m} downstream. The minimum weighted degree is j+q​j+(L−j−1)=L+(q−1)​jj+qj+(L-j-1)=L+(q-1)j with no further insertions, and strictly larger otherwise. The minimum over j≥1j\geq 1 is attained at j=1j=1 and equals L+q−1L+q-1. The linear-only path contributes the leading monomial αL−1​∏mXm​g\alpha^{L-1}\prod_{m}X_{m}g of XX-degree LL. Summing, eq. 22 follows; eq. 23 follows because ∂Xℓ\partial_{X_{\ell}} drops the weighted degree by exactly one on every monomial where XℓX_{\ell} appears. ∎

Lemma 15 implies eq. 6 directly.

Remainder bound for X˙ℓ\dot{X}_{\ell} (eq. 7).

The exact scalar-chain gradient is X˙ℓ=β1​𝔼g​[σ⁡(g)​∂Xℓf]−𝔼g​[f​∂Xℓf]\dot{X}_{\ell}=\beta_{1}\mathbb{E}_{g}[\sigma(g)\partial_{X_{\ell}}f]-\mathbb{E}_{g}[f\partial_{X_{\ell}}f]. For the teacher term, eq. 23 together with Stein’s identity gives

β1​𝔼g​[σ⁡(g)​∂Xℓf]=N​β1​hσ​αL−1​(∏m≠ℓXm)+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−2),\beta_{1}\mathbb{E}_{g}[\sigma(g)\partial_{X_{\ell}}f]=\sqrt{N}\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}\alpha^{L-1}\Bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}\Bigr)+O\bigl(\|X\|^{L+q-2}\bigr),

where the correction comes from the first nonlinear insertion in ∂Xℓf\partial_{X_{\ell}}f paired with σ⁡(g)\sigma(g) and collapsed by Hermite orthogonality. For the self-interaction, eqs. 22 and 23 give |f​∂Xℓf|=O⁡(‖X‖L+(L−1))=O⁡(‖X‖2​L−1)|f\partial_{X_{\ell}}f|=O(\|X\|^{L+(L-1)})=O(\|X\|^{2L-1}). Subtracting,

X˙ℓ=K(σ)​(∏m≠ℓXm)+Rℓ​(X),|Rℓ​(X)|=O⁡(‖X‖min⁡(L+q−2,2​L−1)),\dot{X}_{\ell}=K^{(\sigma)}\Bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}\Bigr)+R_{\ell}(X),\qquad|R_{\ell}(X)|=O\bigl(\|X\|^{\min(L+q-2,2L-1)}\bigr),

with K(σ)=β1​hσ​αL−1/NK^{(\sigma)}=\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}\alpha^{L-1}/\sqrt{N}. For Class B (q=3q=3) and L≥2L\geq 2, L+q−2=L+1≤2​L−1L+q-2=L+1\leq 2L-1, so |Rℓ​(X)|=O⁡(‖X‖L+1)|R_{\ell}(X)|=O(\|X\|^{L+1}), which is the exponent in eq. 7.

Sharpness. The ‖X‖L+1\|X\|^{L+1} order is attained, not just an upper bound. We now identify the degree-(L+q−2)(L+q-2) contribution to RℓR_{\ell} explicitly as coming from the first-activation (j=1j=1) nonlinear insertion, with the form

Rℓ​(X)=qℓ​β1​αL−2​aq​hσ(q)​X1q−1​∏m≠ℓXm+O⁡(‖X‖L+q−1),q1=q,qℓ=1​(ℓ≥2),R_{\ell}(X)=q_{\ell}\beta_{1}\alpha^{L-2}a_{q}h_{\sigma}^{(q)}X_{1}^{q-1}\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}+O\bigl(\|X\|^{L+q-1}\bigr),\quad q_{1}=q,\ q_{\ell}=1\ (\ell\geq 2), (24)

with hσ(q)≐𝔼g​[σ⁡(g)​gq]h_{\sigma}^{(q)}\doteq\mathbb{E}_{g}[\sigma(g)g^{q}]. Every factor of the prefactor is nonzero under the Class B hypothesis. Indeed α=σ′​(0)≠0\alpha=\sigma^{\prime}(0)\neq 0 by the definition of Class B and aq≠0a_{q}\neq 0 by the definition of qq; to see that hσ(q)≠0h_{\sigma}^{(q)}\neq 0, expand σ\sigma and gqg^{q} in probabilist’s Hermite polynomials {hk}\{h_{k}\}, σ⁡(g)=∑k≥1,k​ oddsk​hk​(g)\sigma(g)=\sum_{k\geq 1,k\text{ odd}}s_{k}h_{k}(g) with s1=hσ>0s_{1}=h_{\sigma}>0, and for q=3q=3 use g3=h3​(g)+3​h1​(g)g^{3}=h_{3}(g)+3h_{1}(g) to obtain

hσ(3)=𝔼g​[σ⁡(g)​g3]=6​s3+3​s1=6​s3+3​hσ.h_{\sigma}^{(3)}=\mathbb{E}_{g}[\sigma(g)g^{3}]=6s_{3}+3s_{1}=6s_{3}+3h_{\sigma}.

Appendix C Asymptotic Evaluations and Normal Forms

Here we provide supporting material for Section 4. We give three distinct statements:

  1. (i)

    an exact analytic scalarization of the reduced flow on any nonvanishing open set, provided by the analytic flow-box theorem; this is what makes the one-dimensional quadrature of Theorem 5 exact, and is recorded in Section C.2;

  2. (ii)

    a formal balanced normal form on the punctured cone around the balanced ray, which sharpens (i) into the specific balanced-product shape U˙ℓ=Ψ⁡(U)​∏m≠ℓUm\dot{U}_{\ell}=\Psi(U)\prod_{m\neq\ell}U_{m} with Uℓ=Xℓ+O⁡(sq)U_{\ell}=X_{\ell}+O(s^{q}); this is Theorem 16, and its construction is term-by-term formal series in Section C.1;

  3. (iii)

    an asymptotic near-identity reduction that the escape analysis actually uses: only the first correction (the resonance-detecting term of Corollary 17) and the overall near-identity shift of the upper integration limit are consumed, so the formal series is truncated at low order.

The later subsections use these in combination: Section C.3 proves the (1+o⁡(1))(1+o(1)) accuracy of Theorem 5, the balanced-init scaling (11), the bottleneck-shell decomposition, and the critical-depth law Theorem 6; and Section C.4 handles the Class C universality-breaking coefficient γC\gamma_{C} and the Class D centering device that absorbs a nonzero σ⁡(0)\sigma(0) into a teacher shift.

C.1 Formal Balanced Normal Form

Write the ansatz-reduced vector field of eq. 4 as V=V0+WV=V_{0}+W, where V0=K(σ)∑ℓ(∏m≠ℓXm)∂XℓV_{0}=K^{(\sigma)}\sum_{\ell}\bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}\bigr)\partial_{X_{\ell}} is the leading-order drive and W=O⁡(sL+q−2)W=O(s^{L+q-2}) collects higher-order terms. Use polar-like coordinates XL=sX_{L}=s, Xi=s​1+yiX_{i}=s\sqrt{1+y_{i}} for i<Li<L on the punctured cone

𝒞δ,κ≐{s∈(0,δ),|yi|<κ,i<L}.\mathcal{C}_{\delta,\kappa}\doteq\{s\in(0,\delta),\ |y_{i}|<\kappa,\ i<L\}. (29)

A direct computation gives V0=K(σ)sL−1Ω(y)∂sV_{0}=K^{(\sigma)}s^{L-1}\Omega(y)\partial_{s} with Ω⁡(y)≐∏i<L1+yi\Omega(y)\doteq\prod_{i<L}\sqrt{1+y_{i}} and V0​(yi)=0V_{0}(y_{i})=0, so leading-order transport is pure ss-flow with yy frozen.

Theorem 16 (Formal balanced normal form).

There exist unique formal series Ii​(s,y)=s2​yi+∑n≥q+1sn​Fi,n​(y)I_{i}(s,y)=s^{2}y_{i}+\sum_{n\geq q+1}s^{n}F_{i,n}(y) with Fi,nF_{i,n} analytic in yy, satisfying V⁡(Ii)=0V(I_{i})=0. Setting UL≐sU_{L}\doteq s, Ui≐s2+IiU_{i}\doteq\sqrt{s^{2}+I_{i}} for i<Li<L gives a near-identity change of variables Ui=Xi+O⁡(sq)U_{i}=X_{i}+O(s^{q}) and a formal scalar series Ψ⁡(U)\Psi(U) such that

U˙i=Ψ(U)∏m≠iUm,i=1,…,L,\dot{U}_{i}=\Psi(U)\prod_{m\neq i}U_{m},\qquad i=1,\ldots,L,

to all orders on 𝒞δ,κ\mathcal{C}_{\delta,\kappa}. Consequently Ui2−Uj2U_{i}^{2}-U_{j}^{2} are formal first integrals with leading term Xi2−Xj2X_{i}^{2}-X_{j}^{2}.

Proof sketch.

Matching powers of ss in V⁡(Ii)=0V(I_{i})=0 gives, at order sn+L−2s^{n+L-2}, the homological equation n​K(σ)​Ω​(y)​Fi,n​(y)=−Ri,n​(y)nK^{(\sigma)}\Omega(y)F_{i,n}(y)=-R_{i,n}(y), where Ri,nR_{i,n} is a polynomial in {Fi,m}m<n\{F_{i,m}\}_{m<n} and the σ\sigma-Taylor coefficients. The multiplier n​K(σ)​Ω​(y)nK^{(\sigma)}\Omega(y) is analytic and nonvanishing on the cone, so each Fi,nF_{i,n} is uniquely determined and analytic, with no small-divisor obstruction. By construction Ui2−UL2=IiU_{i}^{2}-U_{L}^{2}=I_{i}, so V⁡(Ui2)=V⁡(s2)≐Θ⁡(U)V(U_{i}^{2})=V(s^{2})\doteq\Theta(U) is ii-independent, and Ψ⁡(U)≐Θ⁡(U)/[2​∏mUm]\Psi(U)\doteq\Theta(U)/[2\prod_{m}U_{m}] realizes the balanced product form. A full proof is omitted since we never require the full formal series. ∎

The content of Theorem 16 is not existence of a flow-rectifying change of variables (which is generic away from critical points) but its specific asymptotic shape: Ui=Xi+O⁡(sq)U_{i}=X_{i}+O(s^{q}) preserves the deep-linear balance law at leading order near the small balanced ray. For 11-homogeneous σ\sigma (linear, ReLU), W≡0W\equiv 0 and Ii=s2​yiI_{i}=s^{2}y_{i} exactly, recovering the classical deep-linear balance Xi2−Xj2=constX_{i}^{2}-X_{j}^{2}=\mathrm{const}.

C.2 Exact Scalarization of the Reduced Flow

The formal balanced normal form is the near-balanced-ray statement; it rests on the fact that the analytic reduced vector field is scalarizable on any nonvanishing open set of the foliation, and that escape time is a one-dimensional quadrature of the resulting scalar speed.

Remark (Analytic scalarization is generic).

Because the analytic reduced vector field VV is nonvanishing on the punctured cone 𝒞δ,κ\mathcal{C}_{\delta,\kappa} of eq. 29, the analytic flow-box theorem provides, locally around any such point, analytic coordinates (U,I1,…,IL−1)(U,I_{1},\ldots,I_{L-1}) in which V⁡(Ii)=0V(I_{i})=0 and V⁡(U)=Θ⁡(U,I)>0V(U)=\Theta(U,I)>0; the flight time on each leaf {I=I0}\{I=I_{0}\} is then the one-dimensional quadrature T(U0→U1;I0)=∫U0U1dU/Θ(U,I0)T(U_{0}\to U_{1};I_{0})=\int_{U_{0}}^{U_{1}}dU/\Theta(U,I_{0}). The core statement is the near-identity form Ui=s2+IiU_{i}=\sqrt{s^{2}+I_{i}}, which is Theorem 16; its consequence for escape times at resonance L=q+1L=q+1 is Corollary 17.

Restricting Theorem 16 to the balanced ray X1=⋯=XL=UX_{1}=\cdots=X_{L}=U and keeping the first nontrivial series term yields the scalar normal form

U˙=K(σ)​UL−1+C1(σ)​UL+q−2+O⁡(UL+2​q−3),\dot{U}=K^{(\sigma)}U^{L-1}+C_{1}^{(\sigma)}U^{L+q-2}+O(U^{L+2q-3}), (30)

with

C1(σ)=β1​aq​αL−1​μq+1N,μq+1≐𝔼⁡[gq+1​σ​(g)]/α,C_{1}^{(\sigma)}=\frac{\beta_{1}a_{q}\alpha^{L-1}\mu_{q+1}}{\sqrt{N}},\qquad\mu_{q+1}\doteq\mathbb{E}[g^{q+1}\sigma(g)]/\alpha,

To derive C1(σ)C_{1}^{(\sigma)}: on the balanced ray with Xℓ=UX_{\ell}=U for all ℓ\ell, a single nonlinear insertion at the first activation replaces the linear branch α​c0=α​U​g\alpha c_{0}=\alpha Ug with aq​(U​g)qa_{q}(Ug)^{q}, propagated through L−1L-1 downstream linear branches each contributing α​U\alpha U. The resulting monomial is N​aq​αL−2​UL+q−1​gq\sqrt{N}a_{q}\alpha^{L-2}U^{L+q-1}g^{q}; pairing with the teacher drive β1​𝔼​[σ⁡(g)⋅gq]=β1​α​μq+1\beta_{1}\mathbb{E}[\sigma(g)\cdot g^{q}]=\beta_{1}\alpha\mu_{q+1} and differentiating in UU produces the coefficient above. The same filtered-composition template of Lemma 15 at general LL ensures no lower-order insertions contribute. The corresponding renormalized escape quadrature on the balanced leaf is then the following.

Corollary 17 (Renormalized escape quadrature on the balanced leaf).

Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 16, and let q≥2q\geq 2 be the degree of the first nonlinear term of σ\sigma. Restrict the formal balanced normal form to the balanced ray U1=⋯=UL=UU_{1}=\cdots=U_{L}=U. Then the scalar normal form may be written as

U˙=K(σ)​UL−1​(1+λ(σ)​Uq−1+ρ⁡(U)),\dot{U}=K^{(\sigma)}U^{L-1}\bigl(1+\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{q-1}+\rho(U)\bigr), (31)

where λ(σ)≐C1(σ)/K(σ)\lambda^{(\sigma)}\doteq C_{1}^{(\sigma)}/K^{(\sigma)} and ρ⁡(U)=O⁡(U2​q−2)\rho(U)=O(U^{2q-2}) as U→0U\to 0.

Fix U∗∈(0,δ)U_{*}\in(0,\delta) small enough that |λ(σ)|​U∗q−1≤1/4|\lambda^{(\sigma)}|U_{*}^{q-1}\leq 1/4 and |ρ⁡(U)|≤Uq−1/4|\rho(U)|\leq U^{q-1}/4 on (0,U∗](0,U_{*}]. Then the normal-form flight time from U=εU=\varepsilon to U=U∗U=U_{*} is

tescNF​(ε,U∗)=∫εU∗d​UK(σ)​UL−1​(1+λ(σ)​Uq−1+ρ⁡(U)),t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{NF}}(\varepsilon;U_{*})=\int_{\varepsilon}^{U_{*}}\frac{dU}{K^{(\sigma)}U^{L-1}\bigl(1+\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{q-1}+\rho(U)\bigr)}, (32)

and the first-correction resummed quadrature

tesc[1]​(ε,U∗)=∫εU∗d​UK(σ)​UL−1​(1+λ(σ)​Uq−1)t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{[1]}(\varepsilon;U_{*})=\int_{\varepsilon}^{U_{*}}\frac{dU}{K^{(\sigma)}U^{L-1}\bigl(1+\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{q-1}\bigr)} (33)

satisfies

tescNF​(ε,U∗)−tesc[1]​(ε,U∗)=O⁡(∫εU∗U2​q−L−1​𝑑U),ε→0.t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{NF}}(\varepsilon;U_{*})-t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{[1]}(\varepsilon;U_{*})=O\left(\int_{\varepsilon}^{U_{*}}U^{2q-L-1}dU\right),\qquad\varepsilon\to 0. (34)

In particular, at the resonance L=q+1L=q+1 the first-resummed integrand expands as U−(L−1)​(1−λ(σ)​Uq−1+⋯)U^{-(L-1)}(1-\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{q-1}+\cdots) whose first correction is −λ(σ)​Uq−L=−λ(σ)​U−1-\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{q-L}=-\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{-1}; this integrates to a log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon) term.

Proof.

The scalar normal form eq. 31 rearranges eq. 30. Separation of variables gives eq. 32. Writing A⁡(U)≐1+λ(σ)​Uq−1A(U)\doteq 1+\lambda^{(\sigma)}U^{q-1} and B⁡(U)≐ρ⁡(U)B(U)\doteq\rho(U), the smallness assumption keeps both AA and A+BA+B bounded away from 00 on (0,U∗](0,U_{*}], so 1/(A+B)−1/A=−B/[A(A+B)]=O(U2​q−2)1/(A+B)-1/A=-B/[A(A+B)]=O(U^{2q-2}). Multiplying by [K(σ)​UL−1]−1[K^{(\sigma)}U^{L-1}]^{-1} and integrating yields eq. 34. ∎

C.3 Escape-Time Accuracy and the Critical-Depth Law

We prove the (1+o⁡(1))(1+o(1)) statement of Theorem 5, the balanced-init scaling law eq. 11, and the shell decomposition that underlies Theorem 6.

Theorem 18 (Balanced-init escape time).

Under balanced initialization Xℓ0=εX_{\ell}^{0}=\varepsilon for all ℓ\ell, the leading-order ODE eq. 7 yields eq. 11. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 the ε\varepsilon-scaling changes at L=3L=3 from logarithmic to polynomial ε−(L−2)\varepsilon^{-(L-2)}.

Proof.

Balanced init sets all Dℓ=0D_{\ell}=0, so the 11-D ODE eq. 8 reduces to Y˙=2​K(σ)​YL/2\dot{Y}=2K^{(\sigma)}Y^{L/2} with Y⁡(0)=ε2Y(0)=\varepsilon^{2}, Y⁡(tesc)=1Y(t_{\mathrm{esc}})=1. Direct integration yields eq. 11. ∎

Exact-to-leading-order accuracy.

Pass to Y≐X12Y\doteq X_{1}^{2} with gaps Dℓ≐Xℓ2−X12D_{\ell}\doteq X_{\ell}^{2}-X_{1}^{2}. At leading order X˙ℓ=K(σ)​∏m≠ℓXm\dot{X}_{\ell}=K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{m\neq\ell}X_{m}, so

Y˙=2​X1​X˙1=2​K(σ)​∏m=1LXm=2​K(σ)​Y​∏ℓ≥2(Y+Dℓ).\dot{Y}=2X_{1}\dot{X}_{1}=2K^{(\sigma)}\prod_{m=1}^{L}X_{m}=2K^{(\sigma)}\sqrt{Y\prod_{\ell\geq 2}(Y+D_{\ell})}.

The leading 11-D ODE eq. 8 is thus exact at leading order. The exact ODE carries two corrections. First, the coordinatewise remainder Rℓ​(X)R_{\ell}(X) of eq. 7, of size O⁡(‖X‖L+1)O(\|X\|^{L+1}), feeds each X˙ℓ\dot{X}_{\ell}; multiplied by X1X_{1} it contributes 2​X1​R1=O⁡(‖X‖L+2)2X_{1}R_{1}=O(\|X\|^{L+2}) to Y˙\dot{Y}. Y˙=2​K(σ)​Y​∏ℓ≥2(Y+Dℓ)+R~​(Y,D),|R~|=O⁡(‖X‖L+2).\dot{Y}=2K^{(\sigma)}\sqrt{Y\prod_{\ell\geq 2}(Y+D_{\ell})}+\widetilde{R}(Y,D),\qquad|\widetilde{R}|=O(\|X\|^{L+2}). (35)

Separating variables,

tescexact=∫Y01d​Y2​K(σ)​Y​∏(Y+Dℓ)⋅11+R~/[2​K(σ)​Y​∏(Y+Dℓ)]=tesclead​(1+O⁡(ε⋆)),t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{exact}}=\int_{Y_{0}}^{1}\frac{dY}{2K^{(\sigma)}\sqrt{Y\prod(Y+D_{\ell})}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+\widetilde{R}/[2K^{(\sigma)}\sqrt{Y\prod(Y+D_{\ell})}]}=t_{\mathrm{esc}}^{\mathrm{lead}}(1+O(\varepsilon_{\star})),

Bottleneck-shell asymptotics.

Both Theorem 6 and the ranking rule for non-balanced initialization rest on the same shell decomposition of the escape integrand.

Lemma 19 (Bottleneck-shell asymptotics).

Fix η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). Let 0<s1≤s2≤⋯≤sL0<s_{1}\leq s_{2}\leq\cdots\leq s_{L} satisfy the uniform ratio bound sj/sj+1≤ηs_{j}/s_{j+1}\leq\eta whenever sj<1s_{j}<1, and set Dℓ=sℓ2−s12D_{\ell}=s_{\ell}^{2}-s_{1}^{2} (with sL+1≐1s_{L+1}\doteq 1). with |Ej​(Y,η)|≤C​L​η2|E_{j}(Y,\eta)|\leq CL\eta^{2} uniformly in YY on shell jj, where CC is an absolute constant. In particular, Ej​(Y,η)→0E_{j}(Y,\eta)\to 0 as η→0\eta\to 0, uniformly in YY and LL.
