Appendix D Off-Manifold Single-Mode Exponent Proofs

This appendix proves Propositions 8, 10 and 11 and records the ε\varepsilon-degree argument that underlies the AM-GM step in the proof of the main theorem. Notation is the same as as in Section 5: γ⁡(W)=𝔼⁡[f​g]\gamma(W)=\mathbb{E}[fg], g≐v1⊤​x∼𝒩⁡(0,1)g\doteq v_{1}^{\top}x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), Gℓ=𝔼⁡[g​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤]G_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[g\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}], T⁡(W)=∑ℓ‖Gℓ‖F2T(W)=\sum_{\ell}\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}, M=maxℓ⁡‖Wℓ‖opM=\max_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}, δℓ=∇zℓf\delta_{\ell}=\nabla_{z_{\ell}}f and hℓ−1=σ⁡(zℓ−1)h_{\ell-1}=\sigma(z_{\ell-1}).

Before the L2L^{2} estimates, we record a uniform positivity fact for the first Hermite coefficient hσh_{\sigma} that is used at every occurrence of the positive drive β1​hσ​T​(W)\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}T(W).

Lemma 20 (Hermite-coefficient positivity for Class B/C).

Let σ∈C1​(ℝ)\sigma\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}) be a Class B or Class C activation as defined in Section 3, so σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0 and σ′​(0)=α>0\sigma^{\prime}(0)=\alpha>0. Then

hσ≐𝔼g​[g​σ​(g)]=𝔼g​[σ′​(g)]>0,h_{\sigma}\doteq\mathbb{E}_{g}[g\sigma(g)]=\mathbb{E}_{g}[\sigma^{\prime}(g)]>0,

with g∼𝒩⁡(0,1)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Proof.

The first equality is Stein’s identity for the Gaussian measure: integration by parts against φ(g)=(2π)−1/2e−g2/2\varphi(g)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-g^{2}/2} gives ∫g​σ​(g)​φ​(g)​𝑑g=∫σ′​(g)​φ​(g)​𝑑g\int g\sigma(g)\varphi(g)dg=\int\sigma^{\prime}(g)\varphi(g)dg, valid whenever σ\sigma is polynomially bounded and σ′\sigma^{\prime} is measurable, which all Class B/C activations satisfy.

For positivity, continuity of σ′\sigma^{\prime} and σ′​(0)=α>0\sigma^{\prime}(0)=\alpha>0 give an open neighborhood (−δ,δ)(-\delta,\delta) on which σ′​(g)≥α/2\sigma^{\prime}(g)\geq\alpha/2. When σ′\sigma^{\prime} is nonnegative everywhere (as for tanh\tanh, erf\mathrm{erf}, GELU, softplus, and sin\sin on (−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\pi/2), and swish on ℝ\mathbb{R} for its standard parameterization), this gives

hσ=𝔼⁡[σ′​(g)]≥α2​Pr⁡(|g|<δ)>0.h_{\sigma}=\mathbb{E}[\sigma^{\prime}(g)]\geq\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\Pr(|g| < \delta)>0.

When σ′\sigma^{\prime} can take negative values, positivity follows from a direct Hermite expansion σ⁡(g)=∑k≥1,odd (or allsk​hk​(g)\sigma(g)=\sum_{k\geq 1,\text{odd (or all}}s_{k}h_{k}(g): hσ=s1=𝔼g​[g​σ​(g)]h_{\sigma}=s_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{g}[g\sigma(g)], which is strictly positive whenever the first Hermite coefficient of σ\sigma itself is positive, which we verify directly for each activation considered in this work. ∎

Remark (No universal quantitative lower bound).

Positivity hσ>0h_{\sigma}>0 is all that the downstream arguments require; a universal quantitative lower bound of the form hσ≥α/2h_{\sigma}\geq\alpha/2 is false under the stated hypotheses. Consider the smooth odd monotone family σδ​(u)≐α⋅(δ​π/2)​erf​(u/δ)\sigma_{\delta}(u)\doteq\alpha\cdot(\delta\sqrt{\pi}/2)\mathrm{erf}(u/\delta), for which σδ′(u)=αe−u2/δ2\sigma_{\delta}^{\prime}(u)=\alpha e^{-u^{2}/\delta^{2}} and σδ′​(0)=α\sigma_{\delta}^{\prime}(0)=\alpha. Direct computation gives hσδ=α/1+2/δ2h_{\sigma_{\delta}}=\alpha/\sqrt{1+2/\delta^{2}}, which is smaller than α/2\alpha/2 for all δ<2/3\delta<\sqrt{2/3}. Any quantitative lower bound on hσh_{\sigma} therefore depends on the specific shape of σ′\sigma^{\prime}, not just on σ′​(0)=α\sigma^{\prime}(0)=\alpha and monotonicity.

Lemma 20 is used wherever the signal-energy identity γ˙=β1​hσ​T​(W)​(1+O⁡(M2))−S⁡(W)\dot{\gamma}=\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}T(W)(1+O(M^{2}))-S(W) is converted to a positive lower bound γ˙≥12​β1​hσ​T​(W)\dot{\gamma}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}T(W); positivity of hσh_{\sigma} is the sign that makes the teacher term a drive rather than a drag.

For any non-bottleneck layer ℓ>r\ell>r, the linear-path tensor expansion gives ‖Gℓ‖F≍∏m≠ℓym\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\asymp\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m}; since exactly rr factors are bottleneck (ym≍‖Wm‖op≤My_{m}\asymp\|W_{m}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq M) and the remaining L−r−1L-r-1 factors are Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) by the initial window on non-bottleneck layers (bootstrapped inductively), we have ‖Gℓ‖F≲Mr\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\lesssim M^{r}. We do not assume monotonicity of M⁡(t)M(t); instead, let V⁡(t)V(t) solve the comparison ODE V˙=C​Vr−1\dot{V}=CV^{r-1} with V⁡(0)=M⁡(0)V(0)=M(0), so that the Dini bound D+​M≤C​Mr−1D^{+}M\leq CM^{r-1} of eq. 49 together with a Petrov–Grönwall comparison gives M⁡(t)≤V⁡(t)M(t)\leq V(t) pointwise on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}]. VV is strictly increasing, so the change of variables t=t⁡(V)t=t(V) is legitimate along VV; bounding M​(t)r≤V​(t)rM(t)^{r}\leq V(t)^{r} and using V˙=C​Vr−1\dot{V}=CV^{r-1} to rewrite d​t=d​V/[C​Vr−1]dt=dV/[CV^{r-1}],

∫0τm0‖W˙ℓ​(t)‖F​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\tau_{m_{0}}}\|\dot{W}_{\ell}(t)\|_{F}dt ≤∫0τm0C′​M​(t)r​𝑑t≤∫0τm0C′​V​(t)r​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\tau_{m_{0}}}C^{\prime}\,M(t)^{r}\,dt\leq\int_{0}^{\tau_{m_{0}}}C^{\prime}\,V(t)^{r}\,dt
=∫V⁡(0)V⁡(τm0)C′​VrC​Vr−1​𝑑V≤C′C⋅m02−V​(0)22≤C∗​m02,\displaystyle=\int_{V(0)}^{V(\tau_{m_{0}})}\frac{C^{\prime}V^{r}}{CV^{r-1}}\,dV\leq\frac{C^{\prime}}{C}\cdot\frac{m_{0}^{2}-V(0)^{2}}{2}\leq C^{\ast}m_{0}^{2},

using V⁡(τm0)≤m0V(\tau_{m_{0}})\leq m_{0} for the upper limit; this gives eq. 43 by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applied to WℓW_{\ell}. Choosing m0∗m_{0}^{\ast} small enough that C∗​(m0∗)2≤c∗/2C^{\ast}(m_{0}^{\ast})^{2}\leq c_{\ast}/2 ensures the non-bottleneck operator-norm and singular-value windows persist, so the linear-path constants used in Definition 9(i),(ii) remain uniform throughout [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}]. ∎

Lemma 22 closes the bootstrap: the non-bottleneck stack drifts by at most O⁡(m02)O(m_{0}^{2}) in Frobenius norm on the entire bootstrap interval, so the assumption that it stays in its initial operator-norm window is not a separate hypothesis but a direct consequence of the small-signal regime M≤m0M\leq m_{0} together with He-normal init. In particular, the linear-path expansion constants used in the upper and lower bounds below are uniform in ε\varepsilon.

Upper bound on τ⋆\tau_{\star} via signal energy.

By the sign-freedom in the teacher direction, replacing v1→−v1v_{1}\to-v_{1} flips the sign of γ\gamma without changing ff or ℒ\mathcal{L}, so we may assume γ⁡(0)>0\gamma(0)>0. On the bootstrap interval [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}], combining Proposition 8 and Lemma 10 gives, using |γ|≤m0r|\gamma|\leq m_{0}^{r} and |S|≤C​|γ|​T|S|\leq C|\gamma|T, the clean lower bound

γ˙≥c​T​(W),c=12​β1​hσ,\dot{\gamma}\geq cT(W),\qquad c=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_{1}h_{\sigma}, (44)

for m0m_{0} small enough; in particular γ\gamma is nondecreasing and, with γ⁡(0)≥cnd​εr>0\gamma(0)\geq c_{\mathrm{nd}}\varepsilon^{r}>0, stays positive throughout [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}]. The linear-path tensor expansion of Lemma 15 gives, uniformly in (L,r)(L,r),

Gℓ=αL−1​Bℓ​Aℓ−1⊤+Rℓ,‖Rℓ‖F≤C​M2​‖Bℓ‖2​‖Aℓ−1‖2,G_{\ell}=\alpha^{L-1}B_{\ell}A_{\ell-1}^{\top}+R_{\ell},\qquad\|R_{\ell}\|_{F}\leq CM^{2}\|B_{\ell}\|_{2}\|A_{\ell-1}\|_{2}, (45)

with A0=v1A_{0}=v_{1}, Aj=Wj​Aj−1A_{j}=W_{j}A_{j-1}, BL=1B_{L}=1, Bℓ=Wℓ+1⊤​Bℓ+1B_{\ell}=W_{\ell+1}^{\top}B_{\ell+1}; consequently ‖Gℓ‖F≍‖Bℓ‖2​‖Aℓ−1‖2≍∏m≠ℓym\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\asymp\|B_{\ell}\|_{2}\|A_{\ell-1}\|_{2}\asymp\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m} with ymy_{m} the bottleneck linear-path gain in layer mm (so ym=Θ⁡(‖Wm‖op)y_{m}=\Theta(\|W_{m}\|_{\mathrm{op}}) for m≤rm\leq r and ym=Θ⁡(1)y_{m}=\Theta(1) for m>rm>r, with constants independent of ε\varepsilon, LL, rr by Definition 9). Then

T⁡(W)=∑ℓ=1L‖Gℓ‖F2≍∑ℓ=1r∏m≠ℓ,m≤rym2.T(W)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}\asymp\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\prod_{m\neq\ell,m\leq r}y_{m}^{2}. (46)

To justify the restriction to ℓ≤r\ell\leq r: by the tensor expansion eq. 45, for any ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\},

‖Gℓ‖F2≍(∏m≠ℓym)2=(∏m≠ℓ,m≤rym)2⋅(∏m≠ℓ,m>rym)2.\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}\asymp\Bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m}\Bigr)^{2}=\Bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell,\,m\leq r}y_{m}\Bigr)^{2}\cdot\Bigl(\prod_{m\neq\ell,\,m>r}y_{m}\Bigr)^{2}.

For a bottleneck layer ℓ≤r\ell\leq r, exactly r−1r-1 bottleneck factors remain in the first product (each Θ⁡(ε)\Theta(\varepsilon)) and all L−rL-r non-bottleneck factors are Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) by Definition 9(i), giving ‖Gℓ‖F2≍M2​(r−1)\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}\asymp M^{2(r-1)}. For a non-bottleneck layer ℓ>r\ell>r, all rr bottleneck factors appear in the first product and L−r−1L-r-1 non-bottleneck factors in the second, giving ‖Gℓ‖F2≍M2​r\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}\asymp M^{2r}: strictly smaller by a factor M2≤m02≪1M^{2}\leq m_{0}^{2}\ll 1. Summing over the L−r≤LL-r\leq L non-bottleneck layers contributes at most L⋅M2​rL\cdot M^{2r}, which is negligible compared to the rr bottleneck contributions r⋅M2​(r−1)r\cdot M^{2(r-1)} once m02≤1/Lm_{0}^{2}\leq 1/L; this is absorbed into the choice of m0m_{0} in the bootstrap. Hence T⁡(W)≍∑ℓ≤r∏m≠ℓ,m≤rym2T(W)\asymp\sum_{\ell\leq r}\prod_{m\neq\ell,m\leq r}y_{m}^{2}, with constants independent of ε\varepsilon.

AM-GM on the rr bottleneck terms gives

∑ℓ=1r∏m≠ℓym2≥r​(∏ℓ=1r∏m≠ℓym2)1/r=r​(∏m=1rym2)(r−1)/r.\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m}^{2}\geq r\Bigl(\prod_{\ell=1}^{r}\prod_{m\neq\ell}y_{m}^{2}\Bigr)^{1/r}=r\Bigl(\prod_{m=1}^{r}y_{m}^{2}\Bigr)^{(r-1)/r}.

Since γ⁡(W)≍∏m=1rym\gamma(W)\asymp\prod_{m=1}^{r}y_{m} by the Hermite identity (using initial nondegeneracy to bound γ\gamma from below and the sign normalization γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 established above), this gives T⁡(W)≥c′​γ2​(r−1)/r=c′​γ2−2/rT(W)\geq c^{\prime}\gamma^{2(r-1)/r}=c^{\prime}\gamma^{2-2/r}. γ˙​(t)≥c​T​(W⁡(t))≥c​c′​γ​(t)2−2/ron ​[0,τm0],\dot{\gamma}(t)\geq cT(W(t))\geq cc^{\prime}\gamma(t)^{2-2/r}\qquad\text{on }[0,\tau_{m_{0}}], (47)

and integrating this hitting-time comparison from γ⁡(0)=Θ⁡(εr)\gamma(0)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{r}) to a fixed γ⋆>0\gamma_{\star}>0 yields

τ⋆≤∫γ0γ⋆d​γc​c′​γ2−2/r=rc​c′​(r−2)γ0−(r−2)/r(1−o(1))=C+ε−(r−2)(1−o(1)).\tau_{\star}\leq\int_{\gamma_{0}}^{\gamma_{\star}}\frac{d\gamma}{cc^{\prime}\gamma^{2-2/r}}=\frac{r}{cc^{\prime}(r-2)}\gamma_{0}^{-(r-2)/r}(1-o(1))=C_{+}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}(1-o(1)).

The integrand γ−(2−2/r)\gamma^{-(2-2/r)} has a singularity at γ=0\gamma=0 whenever r≥3r\geq 3, but the integration interval [γ0,γ⋆][\gamma_{0},\gamma_{\star}] is bounded away from this singularity by γ0=Θ⁡(εr)>0\gamma_{0}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{r})>0; the integral is therefore finite and the antiderivative r2−r​γ(2−r)/r\frac{r}{2-r}\gamma^{(2-r)/r} is evaluated at well-defined endpoints. The blow-up of γ0−(r−2)/r=Θ(ε−(r−2))\gamma_{0}^{-(r-2)/r}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}) as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 is not integrand singularity inside the interval but the polynomial divergence as the lower limit approaches the singular point; this is the mechanism by which τ⋆\tau_{\star} diverges polynomially with ε\varepsilon.

Lower bound on τ⋆\tau_{\star} via bottleneck operator growth.

We estimate ‖W˙ℓ‖F≤‖∇Wℓℒ‖F\|\dot{W}_{\ell}\|_{F}\leq\|\nabla_{W_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}\|_{F} in terms of MM alone. From the squared-loss gradient

∇Wℓℒ=β1​𝔼​[σ⁡(g)​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤]−𝔼⁡[f​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤],\nabla_{W_{\ell}}\mathcal{L}=\beta_{1}\mathbb{E}[\sigma(g)\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}]\ -\ \mathbb{E}[f\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}],

the two terms are controlled by the linear-path expansion eq. 45 plus ‖f‖L2≲Mr\|f\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim M^{r} (filtered composition applied to ff, with rr bottleneck layers and non-bottleneck Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1)). The teacher term is ‖β1​𝔼​[σ⁡(g)​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤]‖F≲‖Gℓ‖F≲Mr−1\|\beta_{1}\mathbb{E}[\sigma(g)\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}]\|_{F}\lesssim\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\lesssim M^{r-1}. The student term is ‖𝔼⁡[f​δℓ​hℓ−1⊤]‖F≤‖f‖L2​‖δℓ​hℓ−1⊤‖L2​(F)≲Mr⋅Mr−1=M2​r−1\|\mathbb{E}[f\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}]\|_{F}\leq\|f\|_{L^{2}}\|\delta_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}\|_{L^{2}(F)}\lesssim M^{r}\cdot M^{r-1}=M^{2r-1}. ‖W˙ℓ‖F≲Mr−1+M2​r−1≲Mr−1\|\dot{W}_{\ell}\|_{F}\lesssim M^{r-1}+M^{2r-1}\lesssim M^{r-1} (48)

while M≤m0≪1M\leq m_{0}\ll 1. Since M⁡(t)=maxℓ⁡‖Wℓ​(t)‖opM(t)=\max_{\ell}\|W_{\ell}(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}} is the pointwise maximum of finitely many locally Lipschitz functions, it is itself locally Lipschitz and admits an upper Dini derivative D+​M​(t)≐lim suph↓0h−1​[M⁡(t+h)−M⁡(t)]D^{+}M(t)\doteq\limsup_{h\downarrow 0}h^{-1}[M(t+h)-M(t)] satisfying

By the a Dini-derivative ODE comparison: let V⁡(t)V(t) solve V˙=C​Vr−1\dot{V}=CV^{r-1} with V⁡(0)=M⁡(0)V(0)=M(0); then any absolutely continuous MM with D+​M​(t)≤C​M​(t)r−1D^{+}M(t)\leq CM(t)^{r-1} and M⁡(0)=V⁡(0)M(0)=V(0) satisfies M⁡(t)≤V⁡(t)M(t)\leq V(t) for all t≥0t\geq 0 on which VV exists (a consequence of the Petrov–Grönwall argument for upper Dini derivatives, replacing differentiability of MM). The separated integral gives V(t)=[V(0)−(r−2)−C(r−2)t]−1/(r−2)V(t)=[V(0)^{-(r-2)}-C(r-2)t]^{-1/(r-2)}, so the first time VV reaches m0m_{0} satisfies

We now fix the loss-threshold constants in the order the quantifiers require. Fix any escape threshold ℒ⋆<ℒ⁡(0)\mathcal{L}_{\star}<\mathcal{L}(0). The filtered-composition expansion for the output gives the pointwise bound ‖f⁡(⋅,W⁡(t))‖L2≤C0​M​(t)r\|f(\cdot\,;W(t))\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{0}M(t)^{r} uniformly on the bootstrap interval, hence ℒ⁡(W⁡(t))≥ℒ⁡(0)−C1​M​(t)r\mathcal{L}(W(t))\geq\mathcal{L}(0)-C_{1}M(t)^{r} for a constant C1=C1​(σ,L,c∗,C0)C_{1}=C_{1}(\sigma,L,c_{\ast},C_{0}) independent of ε\varepsilon and m0m_{0}. Choose m0≤m0∗m_{0}\leq m_{0}^{\ast} small enough that C1​m0r<ℒ⁡(0)−ℒ⋆C_{1}m_{0}^{r}<\mathcal{L}(0)-\mathcal{L}_{\star}; this is a condition on m0m_{0} alone, since C1C_{1} does not depend on m0m_{0}. Then

M⁡(t)≤m0⟹ℒ⁡(W⁡(t))≥ℒ⁡(0)−C1​m0r>ℒ⋆,M(t)\leq m_{0}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal{L}(W(t))\geq\mathcal{L}(0)-C_{1}m_{0}^{r}>\mathcal{L}_{\star}, (50)

so the first time ℒ\mathcal{L} drops to ℒ⋆\mathcal{L}_{\star} satisfies τ⋆≥τm0≥C−​ε−(r−2)\tau_{\star}\geq\tau_{m_{0}}\geq C_{-}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}. Combined with the upper bound, τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}). ∎

D.4 The Shallow-Bottleneck Corners r∈{1,2}r\in\{1,2\}

The machinery of Section D.3 was presented for r≥3r\geq 3 because both polynomial integrals ∫γ−(2−2/r)​𝑑γ\int\gamma^{-(2-2/r)}d\gamma and ∫M−(r−1)​𝑑M\int M^{-(r-1)}dM diverge polynomially in that range. The proof applies exactly the same at r∈{1,2}r\in\{1,2\} up to the single step of integrating the scalar comparison ODEs; only the antiderivative changes.

Proposition 23 (Escape time at r∈{1,2}r\in\{1,2\}).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 11 but with r∈{1,2}r\in\{1,2\} in place of r≥3r\geq 3,

τ⋆={Θ⁡(1),r=1,Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε)),r=2.\tau_{\star}=\begin{cases}\Theta(1),&r=1,\\ \Theta\bigl(\log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr),&r=2.\end{cases} (51)
Proof.

Every step of Section D.3 up to and including eqs. 48, 46 and 44 holds uniformly in r≥1r\geq 1: the linear-path tensor expansion of Lemma 15, the signal-energy lower bound Proposition 8, the self-interaction bound Lemma 10, and Lemma 22 (whose comparison ODE V˙=C​Vr−1\dot{V}=CV^{r-1} still has a unique solution for r∈{1,2}r\in\{1,2\}: V⁡(t)=V⁡(0)+C​tV(t)=V(0)+Ct at r=1r=1 and V⁡(t)=V⁡(0)​eC​tV(t)=V(0)e^{Ct} at r=2r=2, both of which leave the non-bottleneck stack at Frobenius-drift O⁡(m02)O(m_{0}^{2}) on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}] by the same FTC argument). We verify the two corners.

Case r=2r=2 (upper bound). Exactly two bottleneck factors contribute, and eq. 46 gives T⁡(W)≍y12+y22≥2​y1​y2≍γ⁡(W)T(W)\asymp y_{1}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}\geq 2y_{1}y_{2}\asymp\gamma(W) by AM-GM on two terms. Substituting into eq. 44 yields the linear comparison γ˙≥c​c′​γ\dot{\gamma}\geq cc^{\prime}\gamma on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}]; integrating from γ⁡(0)=Θ⁡(ε2)\gamma(0)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{2}) to a fixed γ⋆>0\gamma_{\star}>0,

τ⋆≤∫γ0γ⋆d​γc​c′​γ=1c​c′​log⁡γ⋆γ0=2c​c′​log⁡1ε​(1+o⁡(1))=C+​log⁡(1/ε)​(1+o⁡(1)).\tau_{\star}\leq\int_{\gamma_{0}}^{\gamma_{\star}}\frac{d\gamma}{cc^{\prime}\gamma}=\frac{1}{cc^{\prime}}\log\!\frac{\gamma_{\star}}{\gamma_{0}}=\frac{2}{cc^{\prime}}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(1+o(1))=C_{+}\log(1/\varepsilon)(1+o(1)).

Case r=2r=2 (lower bound). The layerwise gradient bound eq. 48 becomes ‖W˙ℓ‖F≲M\|\dot{W}_{\ell}\|_{F}\lesssim M, so D+​M≤C​MD^{+}M\leq CM and the comparison ODE V˙=C​V\dot{V}=CV with V⁡(0)=Θ⁡(ε)V(0)=\Theta(\varepsilon) integrates to V⁡(t)=V⁡(0)​eC​tV(t)=V(0)e^{Ct}; the first time VV reaches m0m_{0} is

τV,m0=1C​log⁡m0V⁡(0)=1C​log⁡1ε​(1+o⁡(1))≥C−​log⁡(1/ε).\tau_{V,m_{0}}=\frac{1}{C}\log\!\frac{m_{0}}{V(0)}=\frac{1}{C}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(1+o(1))\geq C_{-}\log(1/\varepsilon).

The loss-threshold argument eq. 50 applies unchanged with ‖f‖L2≤C0​M2\|f\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{0}M^{2}, so M≤m0M\leq m_{0} forces ℒ≥ℒ⁡(0)−C1​m02>ℒ⋆\mathcal{L}\geq\mathcal{L}(0)-C_{1}m_{0}^{2}>\mathcal{L}_{\star}, hence τ⋆≥τm0≥C−​log⁡(1/ε)\tau_{\star}\geq\tau_{m_{0}}\geq C_{-}\log(1/\varepsilon).

Case r=1r=1 (upper bound). The sum in eq. 46 has a single term whose bottleneck factor structure is empty, T⁡(W)≍1T(W)\asymp 1 with constants uniform on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}], so eq. 44 gives γ˙≥c1>0\dot{\gamma}\geq c_{1}>0 directly; AM-GM is vacuous. Integrating from γ0=Θ⁡(ε)\gamma_{0}=\Theta(\varepsilon) to γ⋆\gamma_{\star}, τ⋆≤(γ⋆−γ0)/c1=γ⋆/c1​(1+o⁡(1))=Θ⁡(1)\tau_{\star}\leq(\gamma_{\star}-\gamma_{0})/c_{1}=\gamma_{\star}/c_{1}(1+o(1))=\Theta(1).

Case r=1r=1 (lower bound). Now eq. 48 degenerates to ‖W˙ℓ‖F≲1\|\dot{W}_{\ell}\|_{F}\lesssim 1, so D+​M≤CD^{+}M\leq C and V⁡(t)=V⁡(0)+C​tV(t)=V(0)+Ct. The first time VV reaches m0m_{0} is τV,m0=(m0−V⁡(0))/C=m0/C⁡(1+o⁡(1))=Θ⁡(1)\tau_{V,m_{0}}=(m_{0}-V(0))/C=m_{0}/C(1+o(1))=\Theta(1), and the loss-threshold step applies with ‖f‖L2≤C0​M\|f\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{0}M, giving τ⋆≥τm0=Θ⁡(1)\tau_{\star}\geq\tau_{m_{0}}=\Theta(1).

Combining the matching upper and lower bounds in each case yields eq. 51. ∎

Remark (The corners are not a continuation of the polynomial law).

Formally substituting r=2r=2 into ε−(r−2)\varepsilon^{-(r-2)} gives ε0=1\varepsilon^{0}=1, which underpredicts the true log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon) escape time; formally substituting r=1r=1 gives ε+1→0\varepsilon^{+1}\to 0, which is dimensionally inconsistent with an escape time. The polynomial law τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}) is the generic scaling, whereas the corners are the logarithmic and constant limits visible only when the polynomial divergence degenerates. The three regimes align with the antiderivative of y−(r−1)y^{-(r-1)}: y2−r/(2−r)y^{2-r}/(2-r) for r≥3r\geq 3, log⁡y\log y at r=2r=2, and yy at r=1r=1. The r=2r=2 logarithm is the nonlinear analog of the log-plateau observed in deep-linear escape [33], recovered here as the critical case of the polynomial law.

Remark (Scope and mechanism of Theorem 11).

Three features of the preceding argument are worth pointing out:

  1. (i)

    Scope. Theorem 11 treats the single-teacher-mode setting (r∗=1r^{*}=1). The linear-path tensor has the exact rank-one form Gℓ=αL−1​Bℓ​Aℓ−1⊤+RℓG_{\ell}=\alpha^{L-1}B_{\ell}A_{\ell-1}^{\top}+R_{\ell} with ‖Rℓ‖F≤C​M2​‖Bℓ‖2​‖Aℓ−1‖2\|R_{\ell}\|_{F}\leq CM^{2}\|B_{\ell}\|_{2}\|A_{\ell-1}\|_{2} (eq. 45), and A0=v1A_{0}=v_{1} is the aligned teacher direction; no “mode” structure needs to be imposed on {Wℓ}\{W_{\ell}\}. The multi-mode extension, where distinct teacher directions couple through shared layers, is treated by the block-aligned cascade of Appendix E and is not claimed here.

  2. (ii)

    Product structure is an identity, not an alignment assumption. The estimate ‖Gℓ‖F≍‖Bℓ‖2​‖Aℓ−1‖2\|G_{\ell}\|_{F}\asymp\|B_{\ell}\|_{2}\|A_{\ell-1}\|_{2} used in eq. 46 is the rank-one Frobenius identity ‖b​a⊤‖F=‖b‖2​‖a‖2\|ba^{\top}\|_{F}=\|b\|_{2}\|a\|_{2} applied to the leading term of eq. 45. It holds at any configuration of {Wℓ}\{W_{\ell}\} on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}]; there is no cross-layer alignment assumption between Aℓ−1A_{\ell-1} and BℓB_{\ell}, and no requirement that the iterates Wℓ​(t)W_{\ell}(t) lie on (or near) the permutation-symmetric submanifold. The O⁡(M2)O(M^{2}) multiplicative remainder in RℓR_{\ell} is absorbed into the ≍\asymp constants using M≤m0M\leq m_{0}, with m0m_{0} fixed independently of ε\varepsilon.

  3. (iii)

    Time-uniformity from the bootstrap. The linear-path constants in Lemma 15, the self-interaction bound of Lemma 10, and the non-bottleneck window of Lemma 22 are all uniform on [0,τm0][0,\tau_{m_{0}}] by construction. The lower-bound step shows τm0≥C−​ε−(r−2)\tau_{m_{0}}\geq C_{-}\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}, and eq. 50 shows ℒ>ℒ⋆\mathcal{L}>\mathcal{L}_{\star} on this interval, so the escape interval is self-certifying: the window on which the estimates hold is the same window on which the loss remains above threshold. The critical-depth exponent is therefore intrinsic to the small-signal regime.

Concentration at He-normal init.

At He-normal init the non-bottleneck Wℓ∈ℝN×NW_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} have i.i.d. Gaussian entries with variance 2/N2/N; standard Gaussian operator-norm concentration gives ‖Wℓ‖op,σmin​(Wℓ)∈[c∗−1,c∗]\|W_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}},\sigma_{\min}(W_{\ell})\in[c_{\ast}^{-1},c_{\ast}] simultaneously for ℓ>r\ell>r with probability ≥1−e−c1​N\geq 1-e^{-c_{1}N}. The bottleneck layers are rescaled by ε\varepsilon, so M⁡(0)=maxℓ≤r⁡‖Wℓ‖op=Θ⁡(ε)M(0)=\max_{\ell\leq r}\|W_{\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\Theta(\varepsilon) with probability ≥1−e−c​N\geq 1-e^{-cN}. The linear-path constants of Lemma 15 are then uniform in ε\varepsilon on the intersection event, which has probability ≥1−e−c1​N\geq 1-e^{-c_{1}N} by a union bound.

Appendix E Multi-Mode Geometry and Homotopy Proofs

This appendix develops the multi-mode geometry deferred from Section 5. Section E.1 collects the main statements: the per-stage rescaled-profile reduction, the structural instability of the block-mean saddle, and the escape-time homotopy identity. Sections E.4 and E.5 derive the Duhamel equations for the off-block W2W_{2} coupling and the layer-11 cross-block rotations. Section E.6 derives the stage-kk scalar fixed-point equation and verifies the εL−2\varepsilon^{L-2} escape-rate scaling of eq. 52. Section E.7 proves the escape-time homotopy identity via Liouville duality.

E.1 Main Statements: Modewise Profiles, Structural Instability, Homotopy Identity

Modewise escape and rescaled scalar profiles.

Under the block-aligned stage-kk ansatz (derived in Section E.6), the mode-kk breaking amplitude ckc_{k} obeys

d​ckd​t=KL(k,σ)​(ρop​(k)2+ck2)(L−1)/2,KL(k,σ)=βk​hσ​TL​(ρop​(k))N,\frac{dc_{k}}{dt}=K_{L}^{(k,\sigma)}\bigl(\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k)^{2}+c_{k}^{2}\bigr)^{(L-1)/2},\qquad K_{L}^{(k,\sigma)}=\frac{\beta_{k}h_{\sigma}T_{L}(\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k))}{\sqrt{N}}, (52)

with chain moment TL​(ρ)=𝔼g​[∏j=1L−1σ′​(ρ⋅chainj​(ρ​g))]T_{L}(\rho)=\mathbb{E}_{g}[\prod_{j=1}^{L-1}\sigma^{\prime}(\rho\cdot\mathrm{chain}_{j}(\rho g))]. Rescaling by the saddle scale, uk≐ck/ρop​(k)u_{k}\doteq c_{k}/\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k) and Γk≐KL(k,σ)​ρop​(k)L−2\Gamma_{k}\doteq K_{L}^{(k,\sigma)}\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k)^{L-2}, yields u˙k=Γk​(1+uk2)(L−1)/2\dot{u}_{k}=\Gamma_{k}(1+u_{k}^{2})^{(L-1)/2}, so for any normalized threshold θ>0\theta>0 the escape time is

tk(θ)=Γk−1ℐL(θ),ℐL(θ)≐∫0θ(1+s2)−(L−1)/2ds,t_{k}(\theta)=\Gamma_{k}^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{L}(\theta),\qquad\mathcal{I}_{L}(\theta)\doteq\int_{0}^{\theta}(1+s^{2})^{-(L-1)/2}ds, (53)

with ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} depending only on depth; all mode- and configuration-dependence compresses into the single scalar rate Γk\Gamma_{k}. Because ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} is universal, modewise ranking is exact within the reduced model: tj​(θ)<tk​(θ)t_{j}(\theta)<t_{k}(\theta) iff Γj>Γk\Gamma_{j}>\Gamma_{k}. In the small-ε\varepsilon regime, the bottleneck-shell evaluation of Lemma 19 gives ρop​(k)L−2≍εrk−2\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k)^{L-2}\asymp\varepsilon^{r_{k}-2}, where rkr_{k} is the critical depth of mode kk, i.e., the number of layers along the mode-kk saddle cone at scale ε\varepsilon at the start of stage kk, the multi-mode generalization of the rr in τ⋆=Θ⁡(ε−(r−2))\tau_{\star}=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-(r-2)}) of Theorem 5 — so tk​(θ)≍CL(σ)​(θ)/[βk​εrk−2]t_{k}(\theta)\asymp C_{L}^{(\sigma)}(\theta)/[\beta_{k}\varepsilon^{r_{k}-2}]: teacher weight and critical depth trade off linearly in log-time, and a mode of smaller βk\beta_{k} can escape ahead of a larger one if its critical depth is smaller by at least one layer.

Structural instability of the block-mean saddle.

The block-aligned ansatz is exactly flow-invariant from a permutation-symmetric initialization, but the manifold is not attracting at generic Gaussian init. The dominant stage-11 channel in multi-mode simulations is not the off-block W2W_{2} coupling Ck​k′C_{kk^{\prime}} but layer-11 cross-block rotations ηk,m\eta_{k,m}. Augmenting the block-mean ansatz by allowing W1[j,:]=X1,kvk+∑m≠kηk,mvmW_{1}[j,:]=X_{1,k}v_{k}+\sum_{m\neq k}\eta_{k,m}v_{m} for j∈Bkj\in B_{k} and computing the stage-11 Jacobian at the balanced saddle, the reduced-variable equations (derived from the Hermite-moment bookkeeping of Sections E.4 and E.5 — the off-block W2W_{2} and layer-11 cross-block Duhamel derivations, respectively) take the block form

(x˙(1)η˙(1))=εL−2​(−AεBεCε−Dε)​(x(1)η(1))+Rε,\begin{pmatrix}\dot{x}^{(1)}\\ \dot{\eta}^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}=\varepsilon^{L-2}\begin{pmatrix}-A_{\varepsilon}&B_{\varepsilon}\\ C_{\varepsilon}&-D_{\varepsilon}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x^{(1)}\\ \eta^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}+R_{\varepsilon}, (54)

with Aε,DεA_{\varepsilon},D_{\varepsilon} diagonal and positive (the on-diagonal decay rates of each decoupled channel) and Bε,CεB_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon} entrywise nonnegative. The sign structure of Bε,CεB_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon} follows directly from the Hermite-moment expansion of Sections E.4 and E.5: each entry of BεB_{\varepsilon} (resp. CεC_{\varepsilon}) is a leading-order Gaussian expectation of the form c⋅𝔼z​[σ′​(U​z)2​ϕ​(z)]c\cdot\mathbb{E}_{z}[\sigma^{\prime}(Uz)^{2}\phi(z)] with c>0c>0 collecting positive scaling factors (the downstream linear-chain product and the block-size normalization) and ϕ⁡(z)≥0\phi(z)\geq 0 a product of squared pre-activations arising from the cross-block coupling; positivity of σ′​(U​z)2\sigma^{\prime}(Uz)^{2} and of ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z) under the Gaussian measure forces the entry nonnegative. Structurally: a positive η\eta perturbation feeds additional positive pre-activation mass into the xx-channel’s drive, and symmetrically for x→ηx\to\eta; the mutual feedback is manifestly same-sign. By Proposition 25 below, whenever the mixed loop gain ρ⁡(Dε−1​Cε​Aε−1​Bε)\rho(D_{\varepsilon}^{-1}C_{\varepsilon}A_{\varepsilon}^{-1}B_{\varepsilon}) exceeds 11, the decoupled block-mean saddle has a real positive eigenvalue with eigenvector mixing the xx and η\eta blocks, despite all diagonal rates being stabilizing, so it is not structurally stable under layer-11 cross-block rotations. Beyond the block-mean truncation, the stage-11 mean equations couple to arbitrarily high centered row moments Qk(p)Q_{k}^{(p)}: each Hermite expansion of the within-block row distribution feeds into the mean-channel drift through a moment of order qq in σ\sigma, so truncating the hierarchy at row-moment order pp leaves residuals from orders >p>p that are O⁡(εL−2)O(\varepsilon^{L-2}) at the plateau scale: the same scale as the mean-channel drift itself. No finite-moment truncation in the row-moment hierarchy closes the stage-11 mean equations without uncontrolled error at this scale; fully resolving the coupling therefore requires the full row distribution (or a separate argument bounding the high-moment contribution). Under symmetric population gradient descent the row-variance channel is quiescent by symmetry; it reopens under random or stochastic initialization.

The escape-time homotopy identity.

Given that no finite block-mean closure matches the empirical escape time, what we can offer is a principled attribution of the escape-time shift across closure levels. The mechanism is an adjoint-homotopy identity derived from Liouville duality; the proof is in Section E.7.

Proposition 24 (Escape-time homotopy identity).

Let f0=fLOf_{0}=f_{\mathrm{LO}} and f1=faugf_{1}=f_{\mathrm{aug}} be the decoupled and augmented stage-11 vector fields on a common state space, and let fνf_{\nu} (ν∈[0,1]\nu\in[0,1]) be a smooth homotopy between them with the property that escape of the threshold functional h⁡(x)=X1,1−ϑh(x)=X_{1,1}-\vartheta from the shared initial state occurs transversally at a unique time T⁡(ν)<∞T(\nu)<\infty. Let pνp_{\nu} denote the escape-time adjoint along the ν\nu-flow, i.e. the solution of the terminal-value problem p˙ν=−(∂xfν)⊤​pν\dot{p}_{\nu}=-(\partial_{x}f_{\nu})^{\top}p_{\nu}, pν(T(ν))=∇h/(∇h⋅fν)p_{\nu}(T(\nu))=\nabla h/(\nabla h\cdot f_{\nu}). Then TT is C1C^{1} on [0,1][0,1] with

T(1)−T(0)=∫01A(ν)dν,A(ν)=−∫0T⁡(ν)pν(t)⋅(∂νfν)(xν(t))dt,T(1)-T(0)=\int_{0}^{1}A(\nu)d\nu,\qquad A(\nu)=-\int_{0}^{T(\nu)}p_{\nu}(t)\cdot(\partial_{\nu}f_{\nu})(x_{\nu}(t))dt, (55)

where xνx_{\nu} is the fνf_{\nu}-trajectory from the shared initial state.

We view Proposition 24 as a theoretical attribution tool, not a numerical predictor — a direct forward solve at ν=1\nu=1 already returns T⁡(1)T(1). The identity adds an explicit decomposition of T⁡(1)−T⁡(0)T(1)-T(0) into per-channel first-variation contributions A⁡(ν)A(\nu), exposing which channels (off-block W2W_{2} coupling, cross-block rotations, per-layer amplitudes) drive the shift, and where along the homotopy they cancel. Symmetric quadrature evaluates eq. 55 to high order. Figure 5 illustrates the decomposition on a three-mode tanh teacher.

E.2 Structural Instability of the Block-Mean Saddle: Proof

The following proposition supplies an analytic proof that the block-mean Jacobian eq. 54 has a real positive eigenvalue whenever the mixed loop gain exceeds unity. The argument is a continuous-deformation Schur complement driven by the Perron–Frobenius theorem.

Proposition 25 (Schur–Perron positive eigenvalue).

Let A,D∈ℝn×nA,D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be diagonal matrices with strictly positive entries, and let B,C∈ℝ≥0n×nB,C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}_{\geq 0} be entrywise nonnegative. Define

J≐(−ABC−D),ℳ≐D−1​C​A−1​B.J\doteq\begin{pmatrix}-A&B\\ C&-D\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathcal{M}\doteq D^{-1}CA^{-1}B.

If ρ⁡(ℳ)>1\rho(\mathcal{M})>1, then JJ has a real eigenvalue λ⋆>0\lambda_{\star}>0, with a corresponding eigenvector (x⋆,y⋆)(x_{\star},y_{\star}) satisfying x⋆,y⋆≥0x_{\star},y_{\star}\geq 0 and y⋆≠0y_{\star}\neq 0. If in addition ℳ\mathcal{M} is irreducible, then x⋆,y⋆>0x_{\star},y_{\star}>0 and λ⋆\lambda_{\star} is simple.

Proof.

For each λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, the diagonal matrices A+λ​IA+\lambda I and D+λ​ID+\lambda I have strictly positive entries, so they are invertible with nonnegative inverses. Define

K⁡(λ)≐(D+λ​I)−1​C​(A+λ​I)−1​B∈ℝ≥0n×n.K(\lambda)\doteq(D+\lambda I)^{-1}C(A+\lambda I)^{-1}B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}_{\geq 0}. (56)

Entrywise, [K⁡(λ)]i​j=∑kCi​kdi+λ⋅Bk​jak+λ[K(\lambda)]_{ij}=\sum_{k}\frac{C_{ik}}{d_{i}+\lambda}\cdot\frac{B_{kj}}{a_{k}+\lambda}, which is a continuous, strictly decreasing function of λ\lambda on [0,∞)[0,\infty). By continuity of the spectral radius on entries of nonnegative matrices, λ↦ρ⁡(K⁡(λ))\lambda\mapsto\rho(K(\lambda)) is continuous on [0,∞)[0,\infty), and by monotonicity of the Perron root in the entrywise partial order on nonnegative matrices [20, Corollary 8.1.19], λ↦ρ⁡(K⁡(λ))\lambda\mapsto\rho(K(\lambda)) is monotonically nonincreasing.

At λ=0\lambda=0, K⁡(0)=D−1​C​A−1​B=ℳK(0)=D^{-1}CA^{-1}B=\mathcal{M}, so ρ⁡(K⁡(0))=ρ⁡(ℳ)>1\rho(K(0))=\rho(\mathcal{M})>1 by hypothesis. As λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, [K⁡(λ)]i​j=O⁡(λ−2)[K(\lambda)]_{ij}=O(\lambda^{-2}) entrywise, so ‖K⁡(λ)‖∞→0\|K(\lambda)\|_{\infty}\to 0 and ρ⁡(K⁡(λ))≤‖K⁡(λ)‖∞→0\rho(K(\lambda))\leq\|K(\lambda)\|_{\infty}\to 0. Using the intermediate value theorem, there exists λ⋆∈(0,∞)\lambda_{\star}\in(0,\infty) with

ρ⁡(K⁡(λ⋆))=1.\rho(K(\lambda_{\star}))=1. (57)

By the Perron–Frobenius theorem for nonnegative matrices, the spectral radius ρ⁡(K⁡(λ⋆))=1\rho(K(\lambda_{\star}))=1 is an eigenvalue of K⁡(λ⋆)K(\lambda_{\star}), realized by a nonnegative eigenvector y⋆≥0y_{\star}\geq 0, y⋆≠0y_{\star}\neq 0:

K⁡(λ⋆)​y⋆=y⋆,i.e.,(D+λ⋆​I)−1​C​(A+λ⋆​I)−1​B​y⋆=y⋆.K(\lambda_{\star})y_{\star}=y_{\star},\qquad\text{i.e.,}\qquad(D+\lambda_{\star}I)^{-1}C(A+\lambda_{\star}I)^{-1}By_{\star}=y_{\star}. (58)

Define x⋆≐(A+λ⋆​I)−1​B​y⋆x_{\star}\doteq(A+\lambda_{\star}I)^{-1}By_{\star}, which is nonnegative entrywise since (A+λ⋆​I)−1(A+\lambda_{\star}I)^{-1} is diagonal with positive entries and B​y⋆≥0By_{\star}\geq 0. Multiplying eq. 58 by D+λ⋆​ID+\lambda_{\star}I on the left yields C​(A+λ⋆​I)−1​B​y⋆=(D+λ⋆​I)​y⋆C(A+\lambda_{\star}I)^{-1}By_{\star}=(D+\lambda_{\star}I)y_{\star}, i.e.,

Cx⋆=(D+λ⋆I)y⋆⟺Cx⋆−Dy⋆=λ⋆y⋆.Cx_{\star}=(D+\lambda_{\star}I)y_{\star}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad Cx_{\star}-Dy_{\star}=\lambda_{\star}y_{\star}. (59)

Likewise, the definition of x⋆x_{\star} rearranges to

(A+λ⋆I)x⋆=By⋆⟺−Ax⋆+By⋆=λ⋆x⋆.(A+\lambda_{\star}I)x_{\star}=By_{\star}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad-Ax_{\star}+By_{\star}=\lambda_{\star}x_{\star}. (60)

Stacking eqs. 60 and 59:

J​(x⋆y⋆)=(−A​x⋆+B​y⋆C​x⋆−D​y⋆)=λ⋆​(x⋆y⋆),J\begin{pmatrix}x_{\star}\\ y_{\star}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-Ax_{\star}+By_{\star}\\ Cx_{\star}-Dy_{\star}\end{pmatrix}=\lambda_{\star}\begin{pmatrix}x_{\star}\\ y_{\star}\end{pmatrix},

so (x⋆,y⋆)(x_{\star},y_{\star}) is a real eigenvector of JJ with real eigenvalue λ⋆>0\lambda_{\star}>0. The nonnegativity of x⋆,y⋆x_{\star},y_{\star} is inherited from the nonnegative Perron eigenvector and the positivity of (A+λ⋆​I)−1(A+\lambda_{\star}I)^{-1}, BB, CC. If ℳ\mathcal{M} is irreducible, then so is K⁡(λ⋆)K(\lambda_{\star}) (since K⁡(λ⋆)K(\lambda_{\star}) has the same zero pattern as ℳ\mathcal{M} for all λ≥0\lambda\geq 0), and the Perron–Frobenius theorem in irreducible form gives y⋆>0y_{\star}>0 strictly entrywise and the Perron root simple; then x⋆>0x_{\star}>0 follows, and simplicity of λ⋆\lambda_{\star} as an eigenvalue of JJ follows from the analogous simplicity statement for K⁡(λ⋆)K(\lambda_{\star}). ∎

Remark (Converse and tightness).

The proof also gives the converse: if ρ⁡(ℳ)≤1\rho(\mathcal{M})\leq 1, then by monotonicity ρ⁡(K⁡(λ))≤ρ⁡(ℳ)≤1\rho(K(\lambda))\leq\rho(\mathcal{M})\leq 1 strictly for every λ>0\lambda>0, so K⁡(λ)K(\lambda) has no eigenvalue equal to 11 for any λ>0\lambda>0; unwinding the eigenvector construction above, JJ then has no positive real eigenvalue (it can still have eigenvalues with positive real part from complex-conjugate pairs, but those are a separate, stronger instability mechanism). Thus ρ⁡(ℳ)>1\rho(\mathcal{M})>1 is exactly the loop-gain condition for a real positive eigenvalue, and is the natural generalization to block coupling of the scalar criterion b​c/(a​d)>1bc/(ad)>1 from the n=1n=1 case.

Proposition 25 applies to eq. 54 once Aε,Bε,Cε,DεA_{\varepsilon},B_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon},D_{\varepsilon} are identified as the Jacobian blocks extracted from the Hermite-moment expansion of Sections E.4, E.6 and E.5. The required hypotheses (Aε,DεA_{\varepsilon},D_{\varepsilon} diagonal positive, Bε,CεB_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon} entrywise nonnegative) are verified structurally from the Hermite-moment definitions in those appendices: diagonal positivity is the decay-rate sign of each decoupled block; nonnegativity of Bε,CεB_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon} follows from the closed forms (62) and (64), each of whose coupling entries is (positivescalar)⋅𝔼⁡[σ′​(U​z)2⋅(nonnegativeHermitepolynomial)](\mathrm{positivescalar})\cdot\mathbb{E}[\sigma^{\prime}(Uz)^{2}\cdot(\mathrm{nonnegativeHermitepolynomial})]. The residual RεR_{\varepsilon} in eq. 54 is O⁡(εL−1)O(\varepsilon^{L-1}) and strictly higher order in the small-ε\varepsilon scaling; perturbing JεJ_{\varepsilon} by an O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon)-small term preserves the simple positive eigenvalue guaranteed by the proposition, so the linear-instability conclusion transfers to the full nonlinear flow on a neighborhood of the saddle by the stable-manifold theorem.

E.3 A No-Go Theorem: Strict No-Closure of the Row-Moment Hierarchy

The two-block form of Proposition 25 presumes that the Jacobian has already been reduced to a finite 2×22\times 2 block structure J=[−ABC−D]J=\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}-A&B\\ C&-D\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]. In the underlying PDE dynamics, however, the coupling blocks B,CB,C are obtained by truncating an infinite hierarchy of row moments: the within-block row distribution at each layer admits a Hermite expansion pℓ​(w)=∑p≥0Qℓ(p)​H​ep​(w)p_{\ell}(w)=\sum_{p\geq 0}Q_{\ell}^{(p)}He_{p}(w), and the Jacobian acts on the graded Hilbert space ℋ=⨁p≥0ℋp\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\mathcal{H}_{p}, where ℋp\mathcal{H}_{p} is the block of degree-pp coefficients. The finite-dimensional blocks used in the main text correspond to a principal-submatrix truncation to degrees p≤Kp\leq K for some fixed KK. The natural question is whether this truncation is faithful: that is, does the finite Perron root λK\lambda_{K} agree with, or converge finitely to, the infinite-dimensional Perron root λ∞\lambda_{\infty}? Theorem 26 answers in the negative.

Theorem 26 (Strict no-closure).

Let 𝒥:𝒟⁡(𝒥)⊂ℋ→ℋ\mathcal{J}:\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{J})\subset\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H} be a densely defined linear operator on the graded Hilbert space ℋ=⨁p≥0ℋp\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\mathcal{H}_{p} whose matrix representation in the Hermite basis has the Schur block form

𝒥=(−𝒜ℬ𝒞−𝒟),\mathcal{J}=\begin{pmatrix}-\mathcal{A}&\mathcal{B}\\ \mathcal{C}&-\mathcal{D}\end{pmatrix},

with 𝒜,𝒟\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D} diagonal and strictly positive (decay rates), and ℬ,𝒞\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C} entrywise nonnegative in the Hermite basis. Let ℳ≐𝒟−1​𝒞​𝒜−1​ℬ\mathcal{M}\doteq\mathcal{D}^{-1}\mathcal{C}\mathcal{A}^{-1}\mathcal{B} be the loop-gain operator (a bounded, entrywise-nonnegative operator on the off-diagonal grading), and assume ℳ\mathcal{M} is irreducible and has Perron spectral radius ρ⁡(ℳ)>1\rho(\mathcal{M})>1.Assume moreover that the infinite loop-gain operator ℳ\mathcal{M} is compact, that its principal truncations MK=PK​ℳ​PKM_{K}=P_{K}\mathcal{M}P_{K}, canonically embedded in the full sequence space, converge to ℳ\mathcal{M} in operator norm, and that ρ⁡(ℳ)\rho(\mathcal{M}) is a simple isolated Perron eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector whose projection outside every finite degree cutoff is nonzero. For each K≥1K\geq 1, let 𝒥K\mathcal{J}_{K} denote the principal-submatrix truncation of 𝒥\mathcal{J} to degrees p≤Kp\leq K, and let λK>0\lambda_{K}>0 (resp. λ∞>0\lambda_{\infty}>0) denote the Perron positive eigenvalue of 𝒥K\mathcal{J}_{K} (resp. 𝒥\mathcal{J}) supplied by Proposition 25 (resp. its infinite-dimensional analog). Then

λ1<λ2<λ3<⋯<λK<λK+1<⋯<λ∞,\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}<\lambda_{3}<\cdots<\lambda_{K}<\lambda_{K+1}<\cdots<\lambda_{\infty}, (61)

strictly, for every K≥1K\geq 1. In particular, no finite truncation captures λ∞\lambda_{\infty} exactly.

Proof.

Fix K≥1K\geq 1. The Schur reduction of Proposition 25 gives λK\lambda_{K} as the unique positive root of ρ​(KK​(λ))=1\rho(K_{K}(\lambda))=1, where KK​(λ)=(𝒟K+λ​I)−1​𝒞K​(𝒜K+λ​I)−1​ℬKK_{K}(\lambda)=(\mathcal{D}_{K}+\lambda I)^{-1}\mathcal{C}_{K}(\mathcal{A}_{K}+\lambda I)^{-1}\mathcal{B}_{K} is the Perron loop-gain operator restricted to degrees p≤Kp\leq K, and analogously for K+1K+1 and for the infinite-dimensional object. Since 𝒜,𝒟\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D} are diagonal and ℬ,𝒞\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C} are entrywise nonnegative, KK+1​(λ)K_{K+1}(\lambda) is a principal-submatrix extension of KK​(λ)K_{K}(\lambda) with the added row and column entrywise nonnegative.

By the Perron–Frobenius monotonicity theorem for nonnegative matrices used earlier [20, Corollary 8.1.19], the Perron root is monotone under principal-submatrix extension: ρ⁡(KK​(λ))≤ρ⁡(KK+1​(λ))\rho(K_{K}(\lambda))\leq\rho(K_{K+1}(\lambda)) for every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. Irreducibility of ℳ\mathcal{M} lifts to irreducibility of each KK​(λ)K_{K}(\lambda) (the zero pattern is shared), and the strict form of monotonicity under irreducibility with a nonzero added row gives the strict inequality ρ⁡(KK​(λ))<ρ⁡(KK+1​(λ))\rho(K_{K}(\lambda))<\rho(K_{K+1}(\lambda)) at every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 for which the added row of 𝒞\mathcal{C} (or column of ℬ\mathcal{B}) has at least one nonzero entry coupled by irreducibility. By hypothesis ℳ\mathcal{M} couples every grading to the Perron eigenvector (irreducibility), so this strict inequality holds at λ=λK\lambda=\lambda_{K}:

ρ⁡(KK+1​(λK))>ρ⁡(KK​(λK))=1.\rho(K_{K+1}(\lambda_{K}))>\rho(K_{K}(\lambda_{K}))=1.

Since λ↦ρ​(KK+1​(λ))\lambda\mapsto\rho(K_{K+1}(\lambda)) is continuous and strictly decreasing in λ\lambda (by the same entrywise-monotonicity argument used in the proof of Proposition 25, now at level K+1K+1), and tends to zero as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, the unique root of ρ​(KK+1​(⋅))=1\rho(K_{K+1}(\cdot))=1 must lie strictly above λK\lambda_{K}. Hence λK+1>λK\lambda_{K+1}>\lambda_{K}, strictly.

The limit λK→λ∞\lambda_{K}\to\lambda_{\infty} as K→∞K\to\infty, with λK<λ∞\lambda_{K}<\lambda_{\infty} for every finite KK, follows from the same argument applied to the principal-submatrix extension 𝒥K⊂𝒥\mathcal{J}_{K}\subset\mathcal{J}: the Perron root of the infinite-dimensional operator strictly dominates every finite truncation. ∎

Corollary 27 (Escape-time no-closure).

Let τ⋆(K)\tau_{\star}^{(K)} (resp. τ⋆(∞)\tau_{\star}^{(\infty)}) denote the escape time predicted by the KK-truncated (resp. full) row-moment dynamics. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 26,

τ⋆(K)>τ⋆(∞)for every finite ​K,\tau_{\star}^{(K)}>\tau_{\star}^{(\infty)}\qquad\text{for every finite }K,

with strict inequality.

Proof.

The escape time along the unstable direction is τ⋆=λ−1​log⁡(1/ε)⋅(1+o⁡(1))\tau_{\star}=\lambda^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot(1+o(1)) on the linearized flow, and strict monotonicity λK<λK+1<λ∞\lambda_{K}<\lambda_{K+1}<\lambda_{\infty} of Theorem 26 gives τ⋆(K)>τ⋆(K+1)>τ⋆(∞)\tau_{\star}^{(K)}>\tau_{\star}^{(K+1)}>\tau_{\star}^{(\infty)} strictly. ∎

We note that a quantitative rate of the gap λ∞−λK\lambda_{\infty}-\lambda_{K} is to our knowledge, open and is left to future work. This does not affect our work in this paper as we only use the no-go theorem proved above.

E.4 Derivation of the Off-Block W2W_{2} Duhamel Equation

Throughout, the teacher is KK-mode with directions {vk}k=1K\{v_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} and coefficients {βk}\{\beta_{k}\}; the KK-block ansatz partitions the NN hidden neurons of each layer into blocks {Bk}\{B_{k}\} of block size NB≐N/KN_{B}\doteq N/K (distinct from the bottleneck operator scale MM of Section 5, which does not enter this appendix); within each block the rows of W1W_{1} point along vkv_{k} and layers ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 carry a scalar Xℓ,kX_{\ell,k}. The off-block perturbation is the rank-11 entry W2​[i∈Bk,j∈Bk′]=Ck​k′/NW_{2}[i\in B_{k},j\in B_{k^{\prime}}]=C_{kk^{\prime}}/N with k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime}. Our goal is the scalar evolution of Ck​k′​(t)C_{kk^{\prime}}(t) under gradient flow.

Why W2W_{2}.

We work with the off-block entries of W2W_{2} because every deeper layer WℓW_{\ell} (ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3) admits the same type of rank-11 off-block perturbation, but with an additional ρopℓ−2\rho_{\mathrm{op}}^{\ell-2} suppression from passing through ℓ−2\ell-2 layers of the balanced chain before the cross-block leak occurs: at layer ℓ\ell, the upstream block-k′k^{\prime} pre-activation has already been propagated through ℓ−2\ell-2 balanced-chain factors of size ρop​(k′)∼ε\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k^{\prime})\sim\varepsilon each, so the rank-11 coupling coefficient enters the Jacobian blocks B,CB,C of eq. 54 with an extra factor of ρopℓ−2\rho_{\mathrm{op}}^{\ell-2} relative to the ℓ=2\ell=2 case. Layer ℓ=2\ell=2 is therefore the shallowest and dominant contribution to the off-block channel, and deeper layers contribute strictly subleading corrections that are absorbed into the remainder ℛk​k′\mathcal{R}_{kk^{\prime}} of eq. 62. The layer-11 channel is structurally different — a row rotation in vv-space, not an off-block weight entry — and is treated separately in Section E.5.

Fix k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime} and write C≐Ck​k′C\doteq C_{kk^{\prime}}. At layer ℓ=3\ell=3, block kk, the added pre-activation is

Δhi(3)(x)=CN∑j∈Bk′σ(W1[j,:]x).\Delta h_{i}^{(3)}(x)=\frac{C}{N}\sum_{j\in B_{k^{\prime}}}\sigma(W_{1}[j,:]x).

Every row j∈Bk′j\in B_{k^{\prime}} equals X1,k′​vk′⊤X_{1,k^{\prime}}v_{k^{\prime}}^{\top}, so W1[j,:]x=X1,k′zk′W_{1}[j,:]x=X_{1,k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}} with zk′≐vk′⊤​xz_{k^{\prime}}\doteq v_{k^{\prime}}^{\top}x block-dependent only. Writing Uk′≐X1,k′U_{k^{\prime}}\doteq X_{1,k^{\prime}}, the block sum collapses to NBN_{B} identical copies and Δ​hi(3)​(x)=(C/K)​σ​(Uk′​zk′)\Delta h_{i}^{(3)}(x)=(C/K)\sigma(U_{k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}}); the block-size factor NB=N/KN_{B}=N/K cancels against the 1/N1/N normalization, leaving an O⁡(1/K)O(1/K) per-entry contribution. Expanding σ⁡(u)=α​u+aq​uq+O⁡(uq+1)\sigma(u)=\alpha u+a_{q}u^{q}+O(u^{q+1}) about u=0u=0 splits this into a linear piece and a nonlinear defect.

To propagate this perturbation to the output we pass through layers ℓ=3,…,L\ell=3,\ldots,L of the target block kk. Linearizing around the unperturbed trajectory, each layer contributes a multiplicative factor Xℓ,kX_{\ell,k}, defining the downstream product Dk​(X)≐∏ℓ=3LXℓ,kD_{k}(X)\doteq\prod_{\ell=3}^{L}X_{\ell,k}. The contribution to the output projected onto block kk is

Δ​fk​(x)=CK​Dk​(X)​[α​Uk′​zk′+aq​Uk′q​zk′q+⋯].\Delta f_{k}(x)=\frac{C}{K}D_{k}(X)\bigl[\alpha U_{k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}}+a_{q}U_{k^{\prime}}^{q}z_{k^{\prime}}^{q}+\cdots\bigr].

Projecting the gradient and summing over the rank-11 pair (i,j)∈Bk×Bk′(i,j)\in B_{k}\times B_{k^{\prime}}, then evaluating the Hermite moments of zk′​σ​(Uk′​zk′)z_{k^{\prime}}\sigma(U_{k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}}) and zk′q​σ​(Uk′​zk′)z_{k^{\prime}}^{q}\sigma(U_{k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}}) under zk′∼𝒩⁡(0,1)z_{k^{\prime}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), yields

C˙k​k′=−αk​k′​Dk​(X)​Uk′​Ck​k′+βk​k′​Dk​(X)​Uk′q+ℛk​k′​(X,C),\dot{C}_{kk^{\prime}}=-\alpha_{kk^{\prime}}D_{k}(X)U_{k^{\prime}}C_{kk^{\prime}}+\beta_{kk^{\prime}}D_{k}(X)U_{k^{\prime}}^{q}+\mathcal{R}_{kk^{\prime}}(X,C), (62)

with Hermite coefficients

αk​k′=α2K​𝔼zk′​[σ′​(Uk′​zk′)2],βk​k′=aq​αK​𝔼zk′​[zk′q​σ′​(Uk′​zk′)],\alpha_{kk^{\prime}}=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{K}\mathbb{E}_{z_{k^{\prime}}}[\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}})^{2}],\qquad\beta_{kk^{\prime}}=\frac{a_{q}\alpha}{K}\mathbb{E}_{z_{k^{\prime}}}[z_{k^{\prime}}^{q}\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k^{\prime}}z_{k^{\prime}})],

where zk′∼𝒩⁡(0,1)z_{k^{\prime}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), the factor α2/K\alpha^{2}/K (resp. aq​α/Ka_{q}\alpha/K) collects the linear-branch contributions from the target-block downstream chain and the 1/K1/K block-size normalization, and the expectations reduce to standard Hermite moments of σ′\sigma^{\prime}. The remainder is ℛk​k′=O⁡(Dk​Uk′2​C)+O⁡(Dk​Uk′q+1)+O⁡(C2)\mathcal{R}_{kk^{\prime}}=O(D_{k}U_{k^{\prime}}^{2}C)+O(D_{k}U_{k^{\prime}}^{q+1})+O(C^{2}).

Setting C˙k​k′=0\dot{C}_{kk^{\prime}}=0 in the linearized equation gives the quasi-steady balance Ck​k′⋆=(βk​k′/αk​k′)​Uk′q−1C_{kk^{\prime}}^{\star}=(\beta_{kk^{\prime}}/\alpha_{kk^{\prime}})U_{k^{\prime}}^{q-1}; the downstream product DkD_{k} cancels in the ratio, so Φk​k′\Phi_{kk^{\prime}} depends on the source block k′k^{\prime} alone, not on the target chain. Variation of constants on C˙=−a⁡(t)​C+b⁡(t)\dot{C}=-a(t)C+b(t) from Ck​k′​(0)=0C_{kk^{\prime}}(0)=0, with a⁡(s)=αk​k′​Dk​(X⁡(s))​Uk′​(s)a(s)=\alpha_{kk^{\prime}}D_{k}(X(s))U_{k^{\prime}}(s) and b⁡(s)=βk​k′​Dk​(X⁡(s))​Uk′​(s)qb(s)=\beta_{kk^{\prime}}D_{k}(X(s))U_{k^{\prime}}(s)^{q}, gives the Duhamel form

Ck​k′(t)=e−∫0ta(s)ds∫0te∫0sa⁡(u)​𝑑ub(s)ds+(higher-order).C_{kk^{\prime}}(t)=e^{-\int_{0}^{t}a(s)ds}\int_{0}^{t}e^{\int_{0}^{s}a(u)du}b(s)ds+(\text{higher-order}). (63)

On a pre-escape plateau with Uk′​(s)∼εU_{k^{\prime}}(s)\sim\varepsilon and Dk​(X⁡(s))∼εL−2D_{k}(X(s))\sim\varepsilon^{L-2}, the constant-coefficient approximations a∼αk​k′​εL−1a\sim\alpha_{kk^{\prime}}\varepsilon^{L-1} and b∼βk​k′​εL−2+qb\sim\beta_{kk^{\prime}}\varepsilon^{L-2+q} reduce eq. 63 to the elementary closed form Ck​k′​(t)=(βk​k′/αk​k′)​Uk′q−1​(1−e−a​εL−1​t)C_{kk^{\prime}}(t)=(\beta_{kk^{\prime}}/\alpha_{kk^{\prime}})U_{k^{\prime}}^{q-1}(1-e^{-a\varepsilon^{L-1}t}), agreeing with the quasi-steady graph at long times.

E.5 Derivation of the Layer-11 Cross-Block Duhamel Equation

The layer-11 cross-block perturbation ηk,m\eta_{k,m} replaces W1[j,:]=X1,kvk⊤W_{1}[j,:]=X_{1,k}v_{k}^{\top} (j∈Bkj\in B_{k}) with W1[j,:]=X1,kvk⊤+ηk,mvm⊤W_{1}[j,:]=X_{1,k}v_{k}^{\top}+\eta_{k,m}v_{m}^{\top} for m≠km\neq k. The derivation of η˙k,m\dot{\eta}_{k,m} is structurally parallel to Section E.4: linearizing σ⁡(z1​[j])=σ⁡(Uk​zk)+η​zm​σ′​(Uk​zk)+O⁡(η2)\sigma(z_{1}[j])=\sigma(U_{k}z_{k})+\eta z_{m}\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z_{k})+O(\eta^{2}) (with Uk≐X1,kU_{k}\doteq X_{1,k} and zk≐vk⊤​xz_{k}\doteq v_{k}^{\top}x, zm≐vm⊤​xz_{m}\doteq v_{m}^{\top}x independent under the isotropic input law), propagating through the balanced downstream chain D¯k​(X)≐αL−2​∏ℓ=2LXℓ,k\bar{D}_{k}(X)\doteq\alpha^{L-2}\prod_{\ell=2}^{L}X_{\ell,k} (starting at layer 22 since the perturbation enters at layer 11, unlike DkD_{k} of Section E.4 which starts at layer 33), and projecting −∇ηℒ-\nabla_{\eta}\mathcal{L} onto the Gaussian input measure (the cross-block pairing 𝔼⁡[zm​zk′′]=δm​k′′\mathbb{E}[z_{m}z_{k^{\prime\prime}}]=\delta_{mk^{\prime\prime}} selects a single block-mm source term, and the self-interaction contributes a decay) yields

η˙k,m=−α~k,m​(X)​ηk,m+β~k,m​(X)+ℛ~k,m​(X,η),\dot{\eta}_{k,m}=-\tilde{\alpha}_{k,m}(X)\eta_{k,m}+\tilde{\beta}_{k,m}(X)+\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{k,m}(X,\eta), (64)

with α~k,m​(X)=D¯k​(X)2⋅𝔼z​[σ′​(Uk​z)2]+O⁡(ε)\tilde{\alpha}_{k,m}(X)=\bar{D}_{k}(X)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{z}[\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)^{2}]+O(\varepsilon) and β~k,m​(X)=D¯k​(X)​D¯m​(X)⋅μk,m​(U)⋅(positive scalar)\tilde{\beta}_{k,m}(X)=\bar{D}_{k}(X)\bar{D}_{m}(X)\cdot\mu_{k,m}(U)\cdot(\text{positive scalar}), where μk,m​(U)≐𝔼z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[z2​σ′​(Uk​z)​σ​(Um​z)]+Um​𝔼z​[σ′​(Uk​z)​σ′​(Um​z)]\mu_{k,m}(U)\doteq\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[z^{2}\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma(U_{m}z)]+U_{m}\,\mathbb{E}_{z}[\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma^{\prime}(U_{m}z)] is the leading-order cross-block Hermite moment extracted from the Stein-pairing expansion. The first factor 𝔼z​[σ′​(Uk​z)2]\mathbb{E}_{z}[\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)^{2}] is nonnegative as a square. The second factor μk,m​(U)=𝔼z​[z2​σ′​(Uk​z)​σ​(Um​z)]+Um​𝔼z​[σ′​(Uk​z)​σ′​(Um​z)]\mu_{k,m}(U)=\mathbb{E}_{z}[z^{2}\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma(U_{m}z)]+U_{m}\,\mathbb{E}_{z}[\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma^{\prime}(U_{m}z)] is checked to be positive on the pre-escape plateau (Uk,Um>0U_{k},U_{m}>0), for each of the activations used in the paper. For odd σ\sigma (tanh, erf, sin; Class B) the first summand 𝔼z​[z2​σ′​(Uk​z)​σ​(Um​z)]\mathbb{E}_{z}[z^{2}\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma(U_{m}z)] vanishes by parity: z2z^{2} is even, σ′​(Uk​z)\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z) is even (derivative of odd), σ⁡(Um​z)\sigma(U_{m}z) is odd, so the integrand is odd and the Gaussian integral is exactly zero. Positivity of μk,m\mu_{k,m} is then inherited from the second summand alone: the integrand σ′​(Uk​z)​σ′​(Um​z)\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma^{\prime}(U_{m}z) is a product of two even functions, positive at z=0z=0 (where both derivatives equal α>0\alpha>0), and the Gaussian expectation is strictly positive by continuity for small Uk,UmU_{k},U_{m} (explicitly, 𝔼z​[σ′​(Uk​z)​σ′​(Um​z)]=α2+O⁡(Uk2+Um2)\mathbb{E}_{z}[\sigma^{\prime}(U_{k}z)\sigma^{\prime}(U_{m}z)]=\alpha^{2}+O(U_{k}^{2}+U_{m}^{2})), so μk,m​(U)=Um​α2​(1+O⁡(ε2))>0\mu_{k,m}(U)=U_{m}\alpha^{2}(1+O(\varepsilon^{2}))>0 on the plateau since Um∼ε>0U_{m}\sim\varepsilon>0. For non-odd σ\sigma (GELU, Swish, softplus; Classes C/D) both summands contribute nontrivially; direct integration against the Hermite basis at Uk,Um=εU_{k},U_{m}=\varepsilon gives a positive leading coefficient. This is a finite calculation, not a monotonicity hypothesis on σ\sigma, and in particular does not require σ\sigma to be monotone (sin is covered by the odd-parity argument above). Comparing (64) with (62), both are of the form θ˙=−a⁡(X)​θ+b⁡(X)+ℛ\dot{\theta}=-a(X)\theta+b(X)+\mathcal{R} with a⁡(X)≥0a(X)\geq 0 and b⁡(X)≥0b(X)\geq 0, so the Jacobian block Bε,CεB_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon} of eq. 54 inherits entrywise nonnegativity and Aε,DεA_{\varepsilon},D_{\varepsilon} are diagonal positive. On the pre-escape plateau D¯k≍εL−2\bar{D}_{k}\asymp\varepsilon^{L-2}, so every entry of Bε,CεB_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon} is Θ⁡(εL−2)\Theta(\varepsilon^{L-2}) and the Perron loop-gain matrix ℳε≐Dε−1​Cε​Aε−1​Bε\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}\doteq D_{\varepsilon}^{-1}C_{\varepsilon}A_{\varepsilon}^{-1}B_{\varepsilon} (notation of Proposition 25) is O⁡(1)O(1) independent of ε\varepsilon at leading order, verifying the hypotheses of Proposition 25.

E.6 Stage-kk Saddle Fixed-Point Equations

After stages 1,…,k−11,\ldots,k-1 have escaped, the first k−1k-1 modes sit on a post-escape manifold on which the scalars Uj=X1,jU_{j}=X_{1,j} (for j<kj<k) are dependent on the teacher coefficients via the deep-linear balance law UjL−1=βj/K(σ)+O⁡(εq−1)U_{j}^{L-1}=\beta_{j}/K^{(\sigma)}+O(\varepsilon^{q-1}), and the downstream chain along each of these modes has relaxed to the balanced ray. The kkth active mode carries Uk=U∼εU_{k}=U\sim\varepsilon that has not yet escaped, and the downstream chain along this mode sits near the small-balanced cone. Modes j>kj>k are also at O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) but decouple from the kkth stage to leading order through the quasi-steady off-block coupling of eq. 62. The effective gradient flow for UkU_{k} therefore decomposes as U˙k=−∂Ukℒeff(Uk;U1:k−1)\dot{U}_{k}=-\partial_{U_{k}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}(U_{k};U_{1:k-1}).

Expand ℒeff\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}} in powers of UkU_{k} at fixed upstream U1:k−1U_{1:k-1}: the three leading contributions are a residual forcing Fk(U1:k−1)F_{k}(U_{1:k-1}) from the un-fitted modes ≥k\geq k (gradient of the squared loss at Uk=0U_{k}=0), a quadratic Hessian coupling with coefficient Hk(U1:k−1)H_{k}(U_{1:k-1}), and the deep-linear self-drive of the kkth mode’s own imbalance. Collecting higher-order terms into Rk​(U)R_{k}(U),

U˙k=Fk(U1:k−1)−Hk(U1:k−1)Uk+K(σ)UkL−1+Rk(U),\dot{U}_{k}=F_{k}(U_{1:k-1})-H_{k}(U_{1:k-1})U_{k}+K^{(\sigma)}U_{k}^{L-1}+R_{k}(U), (65)

with Rk​(U)=O⁡(UkL+q−2)+O⁡(Uk2​maxj<k​Uj)+O⁡(Uk3)R_{k}(U)=O(U_{k}^{L+q-2})+O(U_{k}^{2}\max_{j<k}U_{j})+O(U_{k}^{3}).

Scaling chain.

Abbreviate ρk≐ρop​(k)\rho_{k}\doteq\rho_{\mathrm{op}}(k). We use the following three scaling relations:

(S1)ρkL−2≍εrk−2,(S2)Uk∼ρk,(S3)Fk,Hk scale as powers of ρk,(\mathrm{S1})\ \rho_{k}^{L-2}\asymp\varepsilon^{r_{k}-2},\qquad(\mathrm{S2})\ U_{k}\sim\rho_{k},\qquad(\mathrm{S3})\ F_{k},H_{k}\text{ scale as powers of }\rho_{k}, (66)

where (S1) is the bottleneck-shell evaluation (Lemma 19) with rkr_{k} the critical depth of mode kk, (S2) is the normalized-profile condition Uk=ρk​ukU_{k}=\rho_{k}u_{k} with uk∈(0,θ)u_{k}\in(0,\theta) (uk=O⁡(1)u_{k}=O(1) on the plateau), and (S3) is established next. All exponents below are expressed in ρk\rho_{k} and converted to ε\varepsilon via (S1) only at the final step.

Derivation of (S3). On the stage-kk block-aligned ansatz, the derivative of the network output in the first-layer scale propagates through the kkth mode’s chain linearly at Uk=0U_{k}=0: ∂Ukf|Uk=0\partial_{U_{k}}f|_{U_{k}=0} equals αL−1⋅(block-size factor)⋅(vk⊤​x)⋅∏ℓ=2LXℓ,k\alpha^{L-1}\cdot(\text{block-size factor})\cdot(v_{k}^{\top}x)\cdot\prod_{\ell=2}^{L}X_{\ell,k}, each of the L−1L-1 downstream layers contributing a factor of scale ρk\rho_{k}, so

∂Ukf|Uk=0=Θ⁡(ρkL−1)⋅(vk⊤​x).\partial_{U_{k}}f\big|_{U_{k}=0}=\Theta(\rho_{k}^{L-1})\cdot(v_{k}^{\top}x).

The residual forcing is the Gaussian expectation of this feature against the un-fitted teacher residual ∑j≥kβj​σ​(vj⊤​x)\sum_{j\geq k}\beta_{j}\sigma(v_{j}^{\top}x); orthogonality vk⟂vjv_{k}\perp v_{j} for j>kj>k selects j=kj=k alone, and Stein’s identity gives

Fk(U1:k−1)=ckβkρkL−1(1+O(εq−1)),ck>0F_{k}(U_{1:k-1})=c_{k}\beta_{k}\rho_{k}^{L-1}\bigl(1+O(\varepsilon^{q-1})\bigr),\qquad c_{k}>0 (67)

(the correction term absorbs O⁡(εq−1)O(\varepsilon^{q-1}) contributions from the fitted residual UjL−1−βj/K(σ)U_{j}^{L-1}-\beta_{j}/K^{(\sigma)}). The Hessian coefficient is the second variation,

Hk(U1:k−1)=𝔼[(∂Ukf|0)2]+O(residual⋅∂Uk2f|0)=O(ρk2​(L−1)),H_{k}(U_{1:k-1})=\mathbb{E}[(\partial_{U_{k}}f|_{0})^{2}]+O(\text{residual}\cdot\partial^{2}_{U_{k}}f|_{0})=O(\rho_{k}^{2(L-1)}), (68)

the dominant contribution being the square of the same feature. Both FkF_{k} and HkH_{k} are independent of UkU_{k}.

Ordering of the three terms on the plateau.

Using (S2) to put Uk∼ρkU_{k}\sim\rho_{k} and (S3) to put Fk=Θ⁡(ρkL−1)F_{k}=\Theta(\rho_{k}^{L-1}), Hk=O⁡(ρk2​(L−1))H_{k}=O(\rho_{k}^{2(L-1)}), each of the three terms in (65) is a power of ρk\rho_{k}:

forcing FkF_{k} = Θ⁡(ρkL−1)\Theta(\rho_{k}^{L-1}),
linear drag Hk​UkH_{k}U_{k} = O⁡(ρk2​L−1)O(\rho_{k}^{2L-1}),
self-drive K(σ)​UkL−1K^{(\sigma)}U_{k}^{L-1} = Θ⁡(ρkL−1)\Theta(\rho_{k}^{L-1}).

The drag is higher order by a factor of ρkL\rho_{k}^{L} relative to both the forcing and the self-drive, i.e. Hk​Uk=O⁡(ρk2​L−1)=O⁡(ρkL)⋅ρkL−1H_{k}U_{k}=O(\rho_{k}^{2L-1})=O(\rho_{k}^{L})\cdot\rho_{k}^{L-1}; since ρk→0\rho_{k}\to 0 as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 by (S1), the drag is asymptotically negligible relative to the other two, and Fk+K(σ)​UkL−1F_{k}+K^{(\sigma)}U_{k}^{L-1} is the effective right-hand side. The forcing Fk>0F_{k}>0 has no dependence on UkU_{k} and seeds escape from any Uk∈[0,θ​ρk]U_{k}\in[0,\theta\rho_{k}]; in particular Uk=0U_{k}=0 is not locally attracting, because the linearization at Uk=0U_{k}=0 is U˙k=Fk+O⁡(ρk2​L−1)>0\dot{U}_{k}=F_{k}+O(\rho_{k}^{2L-1})>0 with Fk>0F_{k}>0 bounded below in ρkL−1\rho_{k}^{L-1}.

Escape time.

On the rescaled state uk=Uk/ρk∈(0,θ)u_{k}=U_{k}/\rho_{k}\in(0,\theta), the effective RHS Fk+K(σ)​UkL−1F_{k}+K^{(\sigma)}U_{k}^{L-1} rescales (using (67) and UkL−1=ρkL−1​ukL−1U_{k}^{L-1}=\rho_{k}^{L-1}u_{k}^{L-1}) to

ρk​u˙k=ck​βk​ρkL−1+K(σ)​ρkL−1​ukL−1+(drag,O⁡(ρk2​L−1)),\rho_{k}\dot{u}_{k}=c_{k}\beta_{k}\rho_{k}^{L-1}+K^{(\sigma)}\rho_{k}^{L-1}u_{k}^{L-1}+(\text{drag},O(\rho_{k}^{2L-1})),

i.e. u˙k=Γk​(1+uk2)(L−1)/2⋅(1+O⁡(ρkL))\dot{u}_{k}=\Gamma_{k}(1+u_{k}^{2})^{(L-1)/2}\cdot(1+O(\rho_{k}^{L})) after absorbing the forcing into the +1+1 and the self-drive into the uk2u_{k}^{2} term inside the bracket (the chain-moment identity of eq. 52 fixes the form of the bracket; the same-order forcing term supplies the constant Γk=KL(k,σ)​ρkL−2\Gamma_{k}=K_{L}^{(k,\sigma)}\rho_{k}^{L-2}). Integrating from uk​(0)=0u_{k}(0)=0 to uk=θu_{k}=\theta,

tk=∫0θd​ukΓk​(1+uk2)(L−1)/2​(1+O⁡(ρkL))=Γk−1​ℐL​(θ)​(1+O⁡(ρkL)).t_{k}=\int_{0}^{\theta}\frac{du_{k}}{\Gamma_{k}(1+u_{k}^{2})^{(L-1)/2}}\bigl(1+O(\rho_{k}^{L})\bigr)=\Gamma_{k}^{-1}\mathcal{I}_{L}(\theta)\bigl(1+O(\rho_{k}^{L})\bigr).

Applying (S1) at the final step,

tk=Θ⁡(Γk−1)=Θ⁡(ρk−(L−2))=Θ⁡(ε−(rk−2)),t_{k}=\Theta\bigl(\Gamma_{k}^{-1}\bigr)=\Theta\bigl(\rho_{k}^{-(L-2)}\bigr)=\Theta\bigl(\varepsilon^{-(r_{k}-2)}\bigr),

with ℐ2​(θ)=arcsinh​(θ)\mathcal{I}_{2}(\theta)=\mathrm{arcsinh}(\theta), ℐ3​(θ)=arctan⁡(θ)\mathcal{I}_{3}(\theta)=\arctan(\theta), and ℐL​(θ)=θ​F12​(12,L−12,32,−θ2)\mathcal{I}_{L}(\theta)=\theta{}_{2}F_{1}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{L-1}{2};\tfrac{3}{2};-\theta^{2}\bigr) for L≥4L\geq 4. The drag correction is O⁡(ρkL)=O⁡(εL⁡(rk−2)/(L−2))O(\rho_{k}^{L})=O(\varepsilon^{L(r_{k}-2)/(L-2)}) relative, absorbed into the (1+o⁡(1))(1+o(1)) of the escape law Theorem 6. The successive ratio tk+1/tk=Γk+1−1/Γk−1=(βk/βk+1)⋅(ρk/ρk+1)L−2t_{k+1}/t_{k}=\Gamma_{k+1}^{-1}/\Gamma_{k}^{-1}=(\beta_{k}/\beta_{k+1})\cdot(\rho_{k}/\rho_{k+1})^{L-2} depends on mode weights and critical depths alone, through (S1).

E.7 Proof of the Escape-Time Homotopy Identity

We prove Proposition 24 via Liouville duality. Let Θν\Theta_{\nu} denote the escape-time function of the fνf_{\nu}-flow: the unique solution of the Liouville transport equation

fν⋅∇Θν=−1f_{\nu}\cdot\nabla\Theta_{\nu}=-1 (69)

with boundary data Θν≡0\Theta_{\nu}\equiv 0 on the threshold hypersurface {h=0}\{h=0\}. Along any fνf_{\nu}-trajectory xν​(t)x_{\nu}(t) starting from the shared initial state x0x_{0}, integrating eq. 69 along characteristics gives the orbit identity Θν​(xν​(t))=T⁡(ν)−t\Theta_{\nu}(x_{\nu}(t))=T(\nu)-t. Evaluating at t=0t=0,

T⁡(ν)=Θν​(x0),soT′​(ν)=∂νΘν​(x0).T(\nu)=\Theta_{\nu}(x_{0}),\qquad\text{so}\qquad T^{\prime}(\nu)=\partial_{\nu}\Theta_{\nu}(x_{0}).

Appendix F Experimental and Numerical Details

All experiments train feedforward networks on the squared loss ℒ=12​𝔼x​[(f⁡(x)−y⁡(x))2]\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{x}[(f(x)-y(x))^{2}] with isotropic Gaussian inputs x∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and a teacher network of the same activation as the student. Population expectations are approximated by drawing a fresh Gaussian batch at every gradient step (no fixed dataset). Unless otherwise noted, training uses the normalized-metric convention: the first-layer learning rate is η\eta and all deeper layers use η/N\eta/N, matching the gradient flow whose fixed-point manifold is the symmetric balanced ansatz of Definition 3. Three initialization schemes appear across the figures: symmetric-aligned (Definition 3), modewise-blocks (partitioning hidden units into teacher-aligned blocks), and He-normal with bottleneck rescaling (standard signal-propagating init with selected layers compressed by ε\varepsilon).

Figure 1 (Exactness of the ansatz reduction).

We train a 44-layer tanh network of width N=64N=64 on a single-mode teacher with d=16d=16 and β1=1\beta_{1}=1, using symmetric-aligned initialization at the unbalanced scale X0=(0.03,0.05,0.07,0.09)X_{0}=(0.03,0.05,0.07,0.09). Full-network gradient descent uses batch size 3276832768 with the normalized-metric per-layer learning rates, run for 120000120000 steps with 2525 evenly spaced snapshots recorded. Panel (a) overlays the population loss from full GD (circles) against the reduced ODE trajectory of Theorem 4 (solid curve); panel (b) does the same for the per-layer scales XℓX_{\ell}. The reduced ODE is integrated via LSODA [19] with relative tolerance 10−1210^{-12} and absolute tolerance 10−1410^{-14}; Gaussian expectations in the ODE right-hand side are computed by 128128-node Gauss–Hermite quadrature.

Figure 2 (Depth scaling and critical-depth law).

We evaluate the closed-form escape integral and the reduced ODE for a tanh teacher–student pair with N=64N=64, d=16d=16, and β1=1\beta_{1}=1. Panel (a) uses balanced initialization Xℓ=εX_{\ell}=\varepsilon for all layers, with ε\varepsilon swept over 2020 log-uniform points in [10−2,10−0.75][10^{-2},10^{-0.75}] and L∈{3,…,6}L\in\{3,\ldots,6\}. Panel (b) fixes L=6L=6 and places r∈{3,…,6}r\in\{3,\ldots,6\} layers at scale ε\varepsilon with the remaining L−rL-r layers at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), over the same ε\varepsilon grid. The closed-form leading-order integral of Theorem 5 is evaluated by adaptive Gauss–Kronrod quadrature with absolute and relative tolerances of 10−1010^{-10}; the integrand singularity at Y=ε2Y=\varepsilon^{2} is regularized by the substitution Y=ε2​e2​sY=\varepsilon^{2}e^{2s}. The reduced-ODE escape times integrate the exact flow of eq. 4 via LSODA, terminated at the first crossing of X1=0.3X_{1}=0.3.

Figure 3 (Universality collapse).

We test five activations — three Class B (tanh, erf, sin) and two Class C (GELU, Swish) — on a 44-layer, width-6464 network with d=16d=16 and a single-mode teacher (β1=1\beta_{1}=1), all under symmetric-aligned initialization. Theory curves are the closed-form escape integral evaluated on a 1414-point log-uniform ε\varepsilon grid over [3×10−3,10−1][3\times 10^{-3},10^{-1}]. Full-network GD empirics use batch size 10241024, step size 0.050.05, and 55 independent seeds per ε\varepsilon value; Class B activations are tested at ε∈[0.03,0.1]\varepsilon\in[0.03,0.1] and Class C at ε∈[0.1,0.316]\varepsilon\in[0.1,0.316] (shifted range, since Class C escapes faster at matched scale). Escape is defined as the first crossing of X1=0.5X_{1}=0.5. Reduced-ODE escape times (diamonds) are computed at the same ε\varepsilon values. Panel (b) rescales all curves by the analytically computed activation constant K(σ)K^{(\sigma)} of Corollary 7, demonstrating the claimed collapse.

Figure 4 (Critical-depth law under random initialization).

We train an 88-layer tanh network of width N=128N=128 on a single-mode teacher with d=16d=16 and β1=1\beta_{1}=1, under He-normal initialization: all layers are initialized with entries drawn i.i.d. from 𝒩⁡(0,2/fan​_​in)\mathcal{N}(0,2/\mathrm{fan\_in}), then the first rr layers are rescaled by ε\varepsilon to create a bottleneck of critical depth rr. Training uses SGD with batch size 512512, a uniform learning rate of 0.010.01 across all layers, and fresh Gaussian inputs drawn each step. Escape is defined as the first step at which the instantaneous loss drops below 0.020.02, approximately 10%10\% of the uninformative baseline 12​Var​(y)≈0.19\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Var}(y)\approx 0.19 (loss-based detection is used because, off the symmetric manifold, the network learns a distributed representation that does not align W1W_{1} with the teacher direction).

Threshold sensitivity. To verify that the fitted slopes are not artefacts of the choice of 0.020.02 we repeated the regression at 0.010.01 (early escape) and 0.050.05 (late escape). Across r∈{3,5,8}r\in\{3,5,8\} the slope estimates shift by |Δ​slope|≤0.08|\Delta\mathrm{slope}|\leq 0.08 and the rr-ordering of the three slopes is preserved. We report the intermediate value 0.020.02 in the main figure.

Disjoint ε\varepsilon windows. We test r∈{3,5,8}r\in\{3,5,8\} with per-rr initialization scales chosen so that escape is feasible within 800000800000 SGD steps: ε∈[0.01,0.3]\varepsilon\in[0.01,0.3] for r=3r=3, [0.06,0.5][0.06,0.5] for r=5r=5, and [0.15,0.5][0.15,0.5] for r=8r=8, with 55 seeds per configuration. The windows are partially disjoint — smaller rr reaches smaller ε\varepsilon before the escape budget is exhausted, while larger rr requires larger ε\varepsilon to fit in the budget — so the three slopes are measured on non-identical ε\varepsilon ranges, and the figure does not directly compare absolute escape times across rr, only the slope of log⁡tesc\log t_{\mathrm{esc}} in log⁡ε\log\varepsilon. The theory reference lines of slope −(r−2)-(r-2) are anchored at the largest-ε\varepsilon data point for each rr, to isolate the scaling exponent from prefactor variation.

Figure 5 (Closure hierarchy).

We train a 44-layer tanh network of width N=60N=60 on a 33-mode teacher with d=16d=16, orthonormal directions, and amplitudes β=(1.0,0.3,0.08)\beta=(1.0,0.3,0.08). Initialization uses modewise blocks: the 6060 hidden units are partitioned into 33 blocks of 2020, each placed on the symmetric-aligned ansatz along its teacher direction at scale ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05. Training runs for 150000150000 steps with batch size 40964096 and normalized-metric learning rates (η/NB\eta/N_{B} with block size NB=N/K=20N_{B}=N/K=20). The two vertical predictions are: (i) the leading-order single-mode escape integral of Theorem 5, and (ii) the escape-time homotopy identity of Proposition 24, evaluated by 22-node Gauss–Legendre quadrature at ν=12±12​3\nu=\frac{1}{2}\pm\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}. At each quadrature node, the forward trajectory x˙ν=fν​(xν)\dot{x}_{\nu}=f_{\nu}(x_{\nu}) and backward adjoint p˙ν=−(∂xfν)⊤​pν\dot{p}_{\nu}=-(\partial_{x}f_{\nu})^{\top}p_{\nu} are integrated jointly. The Jacobian ∂xfν\partial_{x}f_{\nu} is constructed analytically in closed form from the reduced-variable equations of motion (layer scales, off-block amplitudes, cross-block rotations): each Jacobian entry is a polynomial in the reduced state with Gaussian moments of σ\sigma and σ′\sigma^{\prime} appearing as coefficients, and these moments are precomputed by Gauss–Hermite quadrature. We cross-validated the derived Jacobian against JAX reverse-mode autodiff on three random reduced states at tolerance 10−1010^{-10}, obtaining agreement to ≤3×10−11\leq 3\times 10^{-11} in entrywise ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm. The augmented closure (X,Ck​k′,ηk,m)(X,C_{kk^{\prime}},\eta_{k,m}) has 2424 degrees of freedom at L=4L=4, K=3K=3; extending to per-layer cross-block amplitudes adds 1212 further variables. All ODE systems use the same adaptive RK4 integrator with local truncation error below 10−910^{-9}.
